title: How Effective is Stretching for Injury Prevention? A Large-Scale Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sports injuries can impact athletes' availability, threaten their career, and have substantial financial impact. Stretching is commonly used as a prevention strategy. However, controversial evidence, methodological shortcomings, and substantial time elapsed since previous key data syntheses justify performing an updated systematic review.
OBJECTIVE: Our goal was to assess the effects of stretching interventions on injury risk.
METHODS: We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies included humans performing stretching and at least one comparator group; sports-related injury data were required. Studies were identified from six electronic databases (CINAHL Complete, Embase, PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science), reference lists, citation tracking, and consultation with external experts. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane tools. Raw injury data were used to assess odds ratios (OR), with OR < 1 meaning a preventive effect for stretching. Results were presented with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and prediction intervals (PIs). An inverse-variance random-effects model was employed using the DerSimonian and Laird estimator. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.
RESULTS: Over 300,000 records were screened, with 19 studies fulfilling the eligibility criteria (> 9000 participants, > 80% male, age range 14-59 years), of which 15 were used for the meta-analyses. Interventions lasted 4-24 weeks and mostly implemented static unassisted stretching with varying volumes. Half the studies used passive controls, and half used diverse active comparators. Risk of bias was high for ~90% of randomized trials and serious for all non-randomized trials. No injury prevention effect was detected for stretching versus all other comparators (k = 15, n = 9,002; OR = 0.945, p = 0.396, 95% CI 0.828-1.078, 95% PI 0.773-1.155), passive controls (k = 10, n = 6273; OR = 0.923, p = 0.209, 95% CI 0.814-1.046, 95% PI 0.796-1.069), or active controls (k = 6, n = 2744; OR = 1.190, p = 0.312, 95% CI 0.849-1.667, 95% PI 0.738-1.919). Likewise, no injury prevention effect was found for muscle, tendon, and ligament/joint capsule injury risk, or across 19 sensitivity analyses, 3 subgroup analyses, and 3 secondary analyses. GRADE denoted very low certainty of evidence for all outcomes except bone injury risk (low certainty).
CONCLUSIONS: Despite the very low to low certainty of evidence as per GRADE judgments, the data consistently showed no chronic effect of stretching on injury risk across multiple analyses. No study assessed the acute effects of stretching on injury risk. Given the studied samples, these conclusions apply mostly to male participants aged 14-60 years performing static unassisted stretching, with little to no information about other populations or interventions. There is virtually no research using sport-specific stretching exercises. Several other caveats are discussed, as well as implications for practice, policy-making and future research.
REGISTRATION: PROSPERO: CRD42024616532. OSF project ( https://osf.io/umj8h/ ) and registration ( https://osf.io/ybdvw ).

title: Lateral Femoral Condyle Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation Location for Osteochondral Defects of the Knee Is Associated With Selected Patient-Reported Outcome Differences but Not With Graft Reoperation or Failure.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), clinically significant outcome achievement, reoperation, and graft failure after isolated medial femoral condyle (MFC) and lateral femoral condyle (LFC) osteochondral allograft (OCA) transplantation.
METHODS: Consecutive patients who underwent OCA at a single cartilage restoration center from 2003 to 2023 were reviewed. Patients were included if they underwent isolated MFC or LFC OCA transplantation and had preoperative and minimum 2-year postoperative PROMs. When multiple postoperative PROMs were available, the most recent score at or beyond 2 years was used. Cohort-specific minimal clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds were calculated as one-half the standard deviation of the change score. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models were adjusted for graft location, baseline PROM score, follow-up time, age, sex, Workers' Compensation status, athlete status, and laterality. Time to reoperation was compared with Kaplan-Meier/log-rank analysis and Cox regression.
RESULTS: A total of 141 patients were included (MFC: n = 79; LFC: n = 62). Follow-up data were available for 115 patients and averaged 6.2 ± 3.0 years (range, 2.0-16.3 years), with no difference between MFC and LFC cohorts (6.2 ± 2.9 vs 6.2 ± 3.2 years; P = .963). In adjusted linear models accounting for baseline PROM score, follow-up time, age, sex, Workers' Compensation status, athlete status, laterality, and ipsilateral meniscal allograft transplantation status, the LFC recipient site was associated with higher Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) Pain (β = 9.1; 95% confidence interval, 1.2-16.9; P = .024) and KOOS Quality of Life (QoL) (β = 12.3; 95% confidence interval, 1.6-23.0; P = .025) scores. After the same adjustment, the LFC recipient site was associated with greater odds of achieving cohort-specific MCID for KOOS QoL, whereas the corresponding KOOS Pain MCID association was attenuated to nonsignificance (P = .054) once ipsilateral meniscal allograft transplantation was included in the model; other threshold analyses were not significantly different. Reoperation rates were 27.8% for MFC and 29.0% for LFC (log-rank P = .805). Graft failure was rare (MFC, 2.5%; LFC, 0%; P = .504).
CONCLUSIONS: At a minimum 2-year follow-up, the LFC OCA recipient site was associated with higher adjusted KOOS Pain and KOOS QoL scores and higher adjusted odds of achieving cohort-specific MCID for KOOS QoL, an association that persisted after adjusting for ipsilateral meniscal allograft transplantation status. Graft location was not associated with reoperation or graft failure.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective comparative cohort study.
journal: Arthroscopy : the journal of arthroscopic & related surgery : official publication of the Arthroscopy Association of North America and the International Arthroscopy Association

title: Combined anterior cruciate ligament-medial collateral ligament injuries: Favourable outcomes with non-operative management of Grade I injuries and no clear benefit of acute over delayed treatment in Grade II and III Injuries-A multicentre retrospective study of the Francophone Arthroscopic Society.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare medial collateral ligament (MCL) management strategies in patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) for combined anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-MCL injuries. Primary outcomes were functional and return-to-sport measures; the secondary outcome was reoperation-free survivorship at one and three years.
METHODS: A retrospective review of 731 ACLRs performed between January 2020 and June 2022 identified patients with combined ACL-MCL injuries treated with ACLR and either operative or non-operative MCL management. Multiligament injuries and concomitant cartilage or realignment procedures were excluded. Clinical examination included Lachman, pivot-shift and valgus stress testing; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessed MCL and meniscal pathology. Outcomes included International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC), Simple Knee Value (SKV) score, Tegner and ACL-Return to Sport after Injury (RSI) scores. Analyses considered MCL strategy, treatment type and timing (acute, within 12 weeks, vs. delayed). Reoperations, ACL re-rupture, contralateral ACL injury and survivorship were recorded.
RESULTS: A total of 414 patients were included, with a mean age of 30.9 ± 10.2 years and a mean follow-up of 18.5 ± 5.2 months. Of these, 98 patients underwent operative MCL management and 316 were managed non-operatively. Operatively managed patients had more severe clinical instability and more MCL ruptures on MRI. Both groups improved in patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). Operative management was associated with lower IKDC and SKV scores in both unadjusted (p = 0.003 for both) and adjusted analyses (adjusted mean difference -5.51; 95% confidence interval [CI] -8.92 to -2.10; p = 0.002 for IKDC; -7.38; 95% CI -11.91 to -2.85; p = 0.001 for SKV), with no significant associations for ACL-RSI or Tegner. Given greater baseline injury severity in the operative group, this association may partly reflect confounding by indication rather than a true effect of surgery. No statistically significant differences in functional or return-to-sport outcomes were found between acute and delayed surgical treatment for either Grade II or Grade III MCL injuries, though subgroup sizes were small. Reoperation and re-rupture rates were similar between strategies.
CONCLUSION: In combined ACL-MCL injuries, non-operative management of Grade I MCL injuries was associated with favourable outcomes. For Grade II and III injuries, PROMs did not differ significantly between acute and delayed surgical management in this cohort. Subgroup sample sizes for these timing comparisons were small, and the findings should be considered exploratory rather than conclusive. The optimal timing of surgical intervention for higher-grade concomitant MCL injuries remains an open question requiring an adequately powered prospective study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective cohort.
journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's professional football: Higher incidence and distinct injury patterns compared to men.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are more frequent in female football players, but sex-specific differences in injury characteristics remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to analyse sex-specific differences in ACL injury incidence and characteristics in professional football.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study used data from a German national ACL registry ('Kreuzbandregister im Deutschen Fußball'), including professional male (first to third league) and female (first and second league) football players from the 2016/2017 to 2024/2025 seasons. Incidence rates were compared using Poisson regression (incidence rate ratio, IRR) and injury characteristics using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: A total of 459 ACL injuries were analysed (177 female and 282 male). The rate was 1.19 versus 0.69 per 1000 match hours (IRR 1.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-2.13). The difference was most pronounced in the first division (IRR 2.49, 1.82-3.41) and smaller and not significant in the lower leagues (IRR 1.24, 0.93-1.65). Injuries in female players were more often non-contact (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.37) and indirect-contact injuries (aOR 2.92), occurred more often on artificial turf (aOR 5.42) and in national team players (aOR 3.03). Concomitant injury patterns did not differ significantly, except for fewer lateral collateral ligament injuries in women.
CONCLUSION: ACL injury rates are higher in female professional football players, particularly in the first division. The predominance of non-contact and indirect-contact mechanisms supports targeted, sex-specific prevention strategies.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, prospective cohort study.

title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

title: Reliability and Minimal Detectable Change of Training Efficiency Index During Preseason and In-Season Training in Professional Rugby League Athletes.
abstract: Fary, T, Duthie, G, Campbell, P, Jennings, J, Ballard, D, and Johnston, RD. Reliability and minimal detectable change of training efficiency index during preseason and in-season training in professional rugby league athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Training Efficiency Index (TEI) is an integrated method using external and internal loads to monitor responses to the training dose. The aim of this study was to quantify relative and absolute reliability of TEI, comparing daily, weekly, and drill-level TEI measurements. Thirty-nine professional rugby league athletes (26 ± 4 years; 1.86 ± 0.06 m; 97 ± 9 kg) were monitored across the 2025 National Rugby League season. The reliability was assessed in two 4-week blocks during preseason (14 sessions) and in-season (11 sessions). Daily reliability was assessed using 1 prespecified field session per week, weekly reliability was calculated by averaging sessions, and drill-level TEI was calculated from a relatively standardized in-season 13v13 match-simulation training drill. Training Efficiency Index was calculated for each training session using wearable microtechnology, combining 5 different external load variables with Edwards' TRIMP. The reliability was estimated using variance-component linear mixed-effects models with an overall intercept as a fixed effect and athlete as a random intercept. Between-athlete and within-athlete variance were used to derive intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), coefficient of variation, and minimal detectable change (MDC) estimates. Weekly aggregation of TEI was more reliable than daily estimates and more reliable during preseason compared with in-season training. Weekly TEI impulse was most reliable across phases (ICC [95% confidence interval] = 0.86 [0.79-0.89] preseason; 0.79 [0.68, 0.86] in-season), with changes >17% (178.6 TEI impulse units) in preseason and >19% (206.7 TEI impulse units) in-season to exceed the phase-specific MDC. These findings support weekly TEI, particularly TEI impulse, for longitudinal monitoring of training responses in rugby league athletes.

title: Recovery of Running and Technical Match Performance After Adductor Muscle Strain Injury in Male Professional Football Players: A Prospective Cohort Study of 27 Players From One LaLiga Team Across Five Seasons.
abstract: Post return-to-play (RTP) running and technical match performance after adductor muscle strain injury remains unclear. The aim of the present study was to examine recovery of running and technical match performance after RTP following acute adductor muscle strain injury in professional football. This prospective longitudinal cohort study followed players from one team (n = 122) across five seasons (2020/2021-2024/2025). Injuries were recorded by the medical staff and confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging. Match performance variables included playing time, total distance, high-speed running distance (> 24 km/h), number of sprints (> 24 km/h), and offensive and defensive technical actions. First eight matches following RTP were compared with the four pre-injury matches. RTP required unrestricted team training and medical clearance for match selection. Data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations methods, adjusting event counts for the amount of playing time. Of the 122 players, 27 sustained at least one acute adductor muscle strain injury, accounting for 54 injury episodes. At Match 1, time played was -7.1% versus PRE (95% CI -16.7% to +3.5%), total-distance rate -0.4% (-2.4% to +1.5%), high-speed running distance +6.9% (-3.5% to +18.5%), and number of sprints +5.9% (-4.0% to +16.8%); none remained significant after FDR adjustment (p ≥ 0.182; pFDR ≥ 0.817). At Match 8, total passes were 26.5% below PRE (95% CI -50.0% to +7.9%; raw p = 0.116; pFDR = 0.567). Across all Match 1-8 contrasts, only long passes at Match 3 remained significant after FDR adjustment (-15.3%; 95% CI -22.4% to -7.6%; raw p < 0.001; pFDR = 0.022). In conclusion, there was little evidence of systematic population-level impairment in running or technical match performance after RTP. Late passing reductions warrant confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

title: Normative Thresholds for Upper Extremity Functional Testing in Adolescent Athletes: Outcome Measures of Strength.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The use of functional upper extremity measures to guide rehabilitation, reduce injury risk, and inform return-to-play decision-making has increased. However, assessment of these measures has focused primarily on collegiate and adult athletes.
HYPOTHESIS: Normative thresholds would differ by dominance, with stronger values exhibited on the dominant limb.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross sectional.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.
METHODS: Healthy, adolescent athletes who reported participation in either contact or overhead upper-extremity sports completed an upper extremity functional test battery administered in a randomized order. Strength measures of internal rotation (IR) and external rotation (ER) as well as the athletic shoulder (ASH) test were collected in prone using a handheld dynamometer. Descriptive statistics were calculated for all outcome measures with separate analyses for dominant (DOM) and nondominant (NON) limbs. The 15th percentile was computed and used to establish performance thresholds. Strength measures were compared between limbs using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with effect sizes calculated. Descriptive statistics were computed to compare exploratorily male versus female and sport-based performance for all strength measures.
RESULTS: A total of 156 participants (78.2% male; 60.2% contact athletes; age, 16.5 ± 1.2 years; weight, 162.8 ± 39.2 lbs) were included for analysis. Norms and percentile thresholds across tests are presented, with shoulder strength thresholds consistently greater in the DOM limb. DOM IR strength was significantly greater than NON IR strength (P = 0.002). ASH performance was greater in the DOM limb for the I position (180 degrees of shoulder abduction; P < 0.001) and Y position (135 degrees of abduction; P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Performance in healthy, adolescent athletes is influenced by limb dominance and task-specificity and indicates that reliance on collegiate or adult-derived normative values may not be appropriate.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These normative thresholds provide a clinically meaningful framework to guide rehabilitation progression and evidence-based decision-making and will serve as the foundation for future work establishing whether these measures are associated with or predictive of subsequent injury.

title: Risk, Knowledge, and Awareness of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) in Elite Female Volleyball Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a condition caused by low energy availability (LEA) and is associated with adverse health and performance outcomes in athletes. Although volleyball involves considerable physical stress and repetitive jumping, little is known about RED-S knowledge and risk of LEA in elite female volleyball players.
HYPOTHESIS: Elite female volleyball athletes have limited awareness of RED-S, and athletes at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q are more likely to be injured.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Elite female volleyball athletes competing in the Turkish Women's Elite Volleyball League during the 2024-2025 season were recruited. Participants completed an online survey including demographic information, the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), and items assessing knowledge, awareness, and support-seeking behaviors related to RED-S. Athletes were classified as "at risk" for LEA using a LEAF-Q cutoff score of ≥8. Associations between LEAF-Q risk status and injury history during the previous year were analyzed.
RESULTS: A total of 148 athletes participated. The mean LEAF-Q score was 5.50 ± 3.48, and 25% of athletes were classified as at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q. Most athletes (92.6%) reported never having heard of RED-S or the Female Athlete Triad. Athletes identified as at risk by the LEAF-Q were significantly more likely to have sustained an injury in the previous year than athletes not at risk (odds ratio, 7.86; 95% CI, 3.03-20.41).
CONCLUSION: Elite female volleyball athletes demonstrated low knowledge of RED-S, while a substantial proportion were identified as at risk for LEA. LEA risk was associated strongly with injury history, supporting the clinical relevance of LEAF-Q screening in this population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine LEAF-Q screening combined with sport-specific education may facilitate early identification of athletes who may require further clinical evaluation for LEA-related problems and may inform prevention-oriented support strategies in elite female volleyball players.

title: Bone-patellar tendon-bone and quadriceps tendon autografts are associated with a higher 1-year risk of thigh muscle injury after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in competitive male athletes: A retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the association between anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) graft type and subsequent thigh muscle injury in athletes involved in pivoting sports.
METHODS: A retrospective observational study was conducted on 221 ACLRs performed in 199 competitive male athletes involved in pivoting sports, classified according to graft donor site: extensor mechanism (bone-patellar tendon-bone [BPTB] or quadriceps tendon) and flexor mechanism (hamstring tendon). Only athletes who returned to sport and completed a minimum of 12 months of follow-up were included. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed thigh muscle injuries occurring within the first year following the discharge date were identified and classified by muscle group injured and graft type.
RESULTS: Thirty-five athletes (15.8%) sustained at least one MRI-confirmed thigh muscle injury (41 muscle-group-level injuries in total) in the year after discharge from ACLR. Athletes who received a graft from the extensor mechanism had a higher proportion of any thigh muscle injury than those with hamstring grafts (27/133, 20.3% vs. 8/88, 9.1%; absolute risk difference 11.2%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.4-20.0; odds ratio [OR] 2.45, 95% CI 1.12-5.88; p = 0.037). Muscle-group analyses showed no significant differences for hamstring injury or quadriceps injury. All six adductor injuries occurred in the extensor donor group (4.5% vs. 0%), but this difference was not statistically robust. After adjustment, none of the three muscle-group comparisons remained significant.
CONCLUSION: Extensor mechanism grafts were associated with a higher proportion of athletes sustaining any thigh muscle injury in the year following discharge from rehabilitation; although absolute rates were low, no individual muscle group showed a significant difference.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Minimally Invasive Surgery for Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy Using a Double-Row SpeedBridge Repair with Rip-Stop Augmentation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The present video article describes a minimally invasive surgery (MIS) technique utilizing a double-row rip-stop SpeedBridge (Arthrex) repair for the treatment of insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT). This procedure is utilized when nonoperative treatment has failed, with the goal of returning patients to their previous levels of activity while avoiding the complications associated with more open procedures. All products mentioned in the videos are manufactured by Arthrex.
DESCRIPTION: The surgical technique is performed with 4 small incisions-2 distal and 2 proximal. Any Haglund deformity and/or enthesophyte are resected with use of an MIS burr through the 2 distal portals. The central third of the Achilles tendon is partially detached with this resection and is repaired with use of a double-row repair. Proximal anchors are placed, and sutures are passed through the Achilles tendon. Working knotless sutures are tensioned to create a rip-stop suture. The sutures are passed and shuttled to the distal row, creating a double-row repair. The distal row is drilled and tapped. The double-row repair is completed with insertion of distal anchors under appropriate tension.
ALTERNATIVES: Nonoperative treatment is beneficial in the initial stages of the condition and is successful in 60% to 80% of patients1-3. Initial treatment strategies for IAT include RICE (rest, ice, compression, and elevation), nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and physical therapy. Eccentric exercise and extracorporeal shockwave therapy have shown promising results3. Paratendinous injections, such as with platelet-rich plasma, have shown various levels of success and need further evaluation3. When nonoperative treatment has failed, operative treatment is a viable option. The surgical approach should be chosen on a patient-specific basis, as different tendinopathy patterns and different associated osseous and soft-tissue conditions may influence preoperative planning. There are a variety of different surgical techniques that include open, endoscopic, and MIS procedures.
RATIONALE: This MIS technique utilizing a double-row SpeedBridge repair with rip-stop augmentation yields fewer wound complications, less pain, quicker initiation of rehabilitation protocols, and quicker return to sport compared with more invasive techniques. Furthermore, the addition of the rip-stop augment to the double-row SpeedBridge repair improves dynamic mechanical strength and mitigates suture tearing through the tendon4.
EXPECTED OUTCOMES: In our experience, patients who undergo this technique will be weight-bearing in a controlled-ankle-motion boot immediately postoperatively and out of the boot by 6 weeks postoperatively, with progressive return to full activities as tolerated. Our study of 61 patients undergoing the double-row SpeedBridge repair demonstrated favorable outcomes, with Foot and Ankle Disability Index scores improving from a mean of 56.3 preoperatively to 98.62 at 12 months postoperatively and visual analog scale pain scores improving from a mean of 7.25 to 0.476. There were no postoperative ruptures at a mean follow-up of 12.5 months. Eleven patients had minor complications within 3 months, including 6 who reported some central numbness over the Achilles tendon6. We expect these outcomes to improve as surgeons become more comfortable and skilled performing MIS techniques.
IMPORTANT TIPS: Proper patient selection (chronic IAT with Haglund deformity and/or an enthesophyte) will help ensure optimal outcomes.It is important to develop a subcutaneous plane for suture passage.The use of fluoroscopy or a nanoscope is helpful in ensuring that the proper bone is resected with the MIS burr.We have found that the irrigator from the MIS burr can be utilized alongside a Frazier suction tip to help remove excess bone.Suture management is important. Precisely maneuver the sutures at all times; it is very important that the sutures do not get tangled so that the procedure flows efficiently.Make sure to fully tension both sutures in order to place the ripstop.
ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS: NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugMRI = magnetic resonance imagingK-wire = Kirschner wireCI = confidence intervalBID = twice dailyprn = as neededDVT = deep vein thrombosis.

title: Citrulline Malate Ingestion Enhances Muscular Performance During a Selected Hypertrophy Hack Squat Training Protocol.
abstract: Wax, B, Dorgo, S, Montalvo, S, Lyons, B, and Mayo, JJ. Citrulline malate ingestion enhances muscular performance during a selected hypertrophy hack squat training protocol. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined potential ergogenic effects of an oral citrulline malate supplement (CM) during lower-body resistance training. Fifteen resistance-trained men completed a randomized, counterbalanced, double-blind crossover design. Subjects ingested 8.0 g CM or placebo 60 minutes before 8 sets of hack squats at 67% one-repetition maximum to failure with 90-second recovery intervals, repeating the protocol with the alternate treatment 1 week later. Blood lactate before and after exercise, rating of perceived exertion after sets 4 and 8, muscle soreness at 24 and 48 hours, and heart rate and blood pressure at rest and 5 and 10 minutes after exercise were assessed. Hack squat repetition numbers were higher overall in the CM condition (condition effect p = 0.0213), and CM increased total repetitions by 10.7 (95% confidence interval 1.4 to 20.0; p = 0.0265; Hedges' g = 0.61) and total workload by 1,064.7 units (95% confidence interval 84.1 to 2045.4; p = 0.0354; Hedges' g = 0.57). Blood lactate increased after exercise but did not differ by condition. Rating of perceived exertion showed no significant condition effect or Holm-adjusted set-specific difference. Citrulline malate was associated with significantly lower muscle soreness overall and at both 24 and 48 hours after exercise. Heart rate and systolic blood pressure showed condition × time interactions, with Holm-adjusted CM vs. placebo differences at 5 minutes after exercise, whereas diastolic blood pressure showed no significant condition effect or Holm-adjusted time-point difference. Acute CM supplementation may improve lower-body resistance training work capacity and reduce perceived soreness without altering lactate accumulation or perceived exertion.

title: Prevalence and associated factors of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: University athletes face substantial academic, physical, and psychosocial pressures that may heighten vulnerability to psychological distress, despite the perceived mental health benefits of sports participation. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh and to examine how these conditions are associated with lifestyle and sociodemographic factors.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study was conducted from March to September 2025 among 249 university athletes aged 18-26 years at six randomly selected universities in Bangladesh. Data were collected online and in person. Psychological distress was assessed with the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21), and health-promoting lifestyle behaviors were evaluated with the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile II (HPLP-II). Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Spearman's correlations, and binary logistic regression analyses were conducted.
RESULTS: The prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress was 42.6%, 42.6%, and 43.8%, respectively. Depression, anxiety, and stress were significantly associated with relationship status, fatigue, socioeconomic status, smoking, sleep duration, sports participation frequency, and satisfaction with sports (all p < 0.05). Participants with depression, anxiety, and stress had significantly lower scores across all HPLP-II domains (all p < 0.01). Higher physical activity was independently associated with lower odds of depression (OR = 0.462, 95% CI: 0.286-0.746), anxiety (OR = 0.756, 95% CI: 0.677-0.845), and stress (OR = 0.773, 95% CI: 0.677-0.882). Better stress management and stronger interpersonal relationships were also significantly associated, whereas other factors were not.
CONCLUSIONS: Depression, anxiety, and stress were highly prevalent among university athletes in Bangladesh and strongly associated with modifiable lifestyle factors. These findings support integrated, athlete-centered mental health strategies emphasizing physical activity, stress management, and psychosocial support. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and determination of the directionality of these associations.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Sex Differences in Psychological Traits, Training Volume, and Dietary Food-Frequency Patterns in Athletes: Associations with Body Dissatisfaction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychological traits, training volume, and dietary behaviors have been associated with body-image and eating-related outcomes in athletes, but evidence integrating these domains from a sex-based perspective remains limited.
OBJECTIVES: This study examined sex differences in psychological traits, weekly training volume, and study-specific dietary food-frequency scores, and evaluated their associations with body dissatisfaction assessed using the Body Dissatisfaction subscale of the Eating Disorder Inventory (EDI).
METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted in 58 athletes (23 women and 35 men). Participants completed questionnaires assessing personality traits, psychological inflexibility, anxiety, loneliness, training characteristics, dietary food-frequency patterns, and body dissatisfaction. Weekly training volume was calculated as the sum of weekly minutes across three intensity zones (Z1 + Z2 + Z3). Analyses included descriptive statistics, Welch's t-tests, Pearson and Spearman correlations, and a hypothesis-driven multivariable ordinary least squares model.
RESULTS: Female athletes had higher EDI Body Dissatisfaction scores and neuroticism than male athletes. Female athletes also had a higher non-pro-inflammatory food-frequency score (22.83 ± 6.31 vs. 19.34 ± 5.50; p = 0.036), whereas the pro-inflammatory food-frequency score did not differ significantly by sex (p = 0.327). Weekly training volume did not differ by sex and was not significantly associated with body dissatisfaction within either sex. In the multivariable model, female sex (B = 2.615, p = 0.036) and the pro-inflammatory food-frequency score (B = 0.308, p = 0.048) were positively associated with EDI Body Dissatisfaction scores; BMI showed an imprecise positive estimate in both the primary and age-adjusted models, whereas neuroticism, weekly training volume, and the non-pro-inflammatory food-frequency score were not independently associated. Model fit was modest (adjusted R2 = 0.180; 5-fold cross-validated R2 = 0.058 ± 0.333).
CONCLUSIONS: Women in this sample reported greater body dissatisfaction and neuroticism. The association between the study-specific pro-inflammatory food-frequency score and body dissatisfaction was small and exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal dietary effect or of biological inflammatory exposure. Larger studies with sport-type information, validated dietary indices, and objective training-load measures are required to test these associations.

title: Adaptive training load optimization for sprinters via offline reinforcement learning and multi-modal physiological feedback.
abstract: Elite sprint training requires daily adjustment of training load to balance performance adaptation and fatigue, yet physiological monitoring does not necessarily translate into a specific next-session prescription. This study formalizes daily sprint training prescription as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process and develops an adaptive load-optimization framework that couples multi-modal physiological feedback with offline reinforcement learning (RL). A 19-dimensional state fusing autonomic, neuromuscular, endocrine, subjective, and load-aggregate signals is encoded by a dual-tower network [a one-dimensional convolutional neural network-Transformer temporal branch and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) static branch] over an action space of 62 admissible training-type/intensity/volume combinations. A composite reward penalizes overreaching while rewarding short-term gain, longitudinal adaptation, and acute-to-chronic workload ratio conformity. The policy is learned by conservative off-policy training on retrospective data, evaluated through the Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and Doubly Robust (DR) estimators, and presented to coaches as the three leading candidate actions, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values used to explain the model's preferences among the candidate actions. In a 12-week single-center retrospective comparison of 70 national-level sprinters (35 men and 35 women; 100 m personal best (PB) ≤ 11.20 s for men or ≤ 12.50 s for women), grouped by whether their squad had adopted the tool (n = 35 RL-guided) or continued classical block periodisation (n = 35 control), the RL-guided cohort demonstrated between-cohort differences of +0.240 s in 100 m [95% confidence interval (CI) +0.128 to +0.352; p < 0.001, d = 1.00], +0.104 s in 30 m (p < 0.001, d = 1.00) and +2.17 cm in countermovement jump (p < 0.001, d = 1.01). Zero algorithmically defined sustained multi-indicator fatigue/load events were observed in the RL-guided cohort vs. seven in the control cohort (1.43 per 1,000 athlete-days); these events should not be interpreted as clinically diagnosed overtraining syndrome. Off-policy evaluation yielded exploratory point estimates whose precision remains unknown because uncertainty intervals were not calculated. These observational findings describe associations with an RL-guided, coach-in-the-loop workflow and do not establish a causal effect of the RL policy.

title: Collective case study on periodized training in elite female middle- and long-distance swimmers preparing for national competition.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elite swimmers increasingly face calendars requiring multiple performance peaks within a single season, a scenario for which traditional single-target periodization models may be insufficient.
METHODS: This longitudinal collective case study followed five elite female middle- and long-distance freestyle swimmers across a 52-week macrocycle preparing for two national championships. The program combined three altitude camps, sea-level integration phases and two timed tapers. Training intensity distribution (TID) was quantified with a three-zone lactate-threshold model; hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cell count, creatine kinase and cortisol were measured at four time points; and performance was assessed by time-trial and official competition results. Given N = 5, analysis prioritized a smallest-worthwhile-change (SWC) classification for performance and paired effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for blood markers rather than null-hypothesis significance testing. Hematological outcomes are concentration-based indices; training-load descriptors refer to in-water swimming only.
RESULTS: Applying an SWC of ≈0.24% to the 20 athlete-by-event observations, 12/20 (60%) changes at Competition 1 and 18/20 (90%) at Competition 2 exceeded the SWC, most representing improvement over baseline; this ordering held across the full defensible range of reference variability (SWC 0.22-0.42%). Hematological effect sizes were largest at Week 27 (RBC: Hedges' g = 2.32, 95% CI [0.64, 4.01]; HCT: g = 2.04 [0.50, 3.58]), while creatine kinase and cortisol peaked at Week 17 and were closer to baseline at Week 49, compatible with a lower physiological stress state at that sampled time point. TID shifted across phases (pyramidal during base development, polarized during altitude blocks, threshold-oriented during race-pace sharpening), with marked inter-individual heterogeneity in performance and physiological responses.
CONCLUSION: Across this double-peak macrocycle, most athlete-by-event changes exceeded the SWC, and the proportion doing so was higher at the second championship than at the first; these changes occurred alongside altitude-associated increases in concentration-based oxygen-transport indices and a taper-associated normalization of creatine kinase and cortisol. With no control group or randomization, only five athletes and four blood samples, several simultaneous interventions and unmeasured confounders (iron status, menstrual-cycle phase, dryland load), these findings describe associations only. They are offered as exploratory, hypothesis-generating observations from a single elite squad rather than as causal evidence.

title: Exercise Endurance Effects of Food-Derived Polysaccharides in Animal Models of Exercise-Induced Fatigue: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The effects of food-derived polysaccharides on endurance may depend on their source materials, extraction and purification procedures, molecular characteristics, and mode of administration; however, their average effects and transferability across animal models remain uncertain. To quantify effects on exercise endurance and to evaluate how chemical/process characterization, biochemical response domains, and evidence quality support functional-food interpretation. Controlled animal studies were systematically reviewed; 31 independent StudyIDs from 30 reports were synthesized using random-effects response ratios (RoM) with Hartung-Knapp intervals. Chemical and processing descriptors and selected biochemical outcomes were mapped as structured evidence layers. Endurance increased overall (RoM 1.707, 95% CI 1.540-1.892; I 2 = 95.4%), while the 95% prediction interval (0.999-2.917) included the null. Characterization was incomplete: purity/content, molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, and extraction or purification information were recoverable for only subsets of StudyIDs. Biochemical observations clustered around energy-substrate, lactate/BUN, oxidative-stress, muscle-injury, mitochondrial/AMPK, and gut-microbiota domains, but few comparable records were suitable for effect-size calculation. Food-derived polysaccharides show a positive average preclinical endurance signal, but very high heterogeneity, incomplete chemical/process reporting, evidence asymmetry, and sparse harmonized biochemical data constrain claims of efficacy for formulated functional foods.

title: Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (aronia melanocarpa) supplementation modulates exercise-induced changes in iron metabolism in female swimmers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intense exercise may transiently alter iron metabolism through inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms. Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) may influence these responses and short-term iron regulation. This study evaluated the effects of black chokeberry supplementation on iron metabolism, inflammation, antioxidant capacity, and hematological status in female competitive swimmers.
METHODS: Twenty-two female swimmers (13.14 ± 1.42 years) were randomly allocated to a supplementation or placebo group. Participants completed two identical swimming tests comprising 800-, 200-, and 50-m efforts before and after 57.32 ± 8.31 days of supplementation. Blood was collected before exercise, immediately after exercise, and after 3 h of recovery.
RESULTS: Most inflammatory markers showed time-dependent changes without significant group effects. C-reactive protein decreased from pre- to post-exercise during the second test in the supplemented group (p = 0.0325; Cohen's d = 1.29), whereas placebo recovery values increased between tests (p < 0.0001; Cohen's d = 3.33). Total antioxidant capacity showed a significant time × group interaction (p = 0.0007), with higher recovery values in the supplemented group. Iron, unsaturated iron-binding capacity, and total iron-binding capacity showed significant time effects (all p < 0.0001). Hepcidin also showed a significant time effect, with significant within-group increases only in the placebo group. Transferrin was lower in the supplemented group at Post II (p = 0.0071; Cohen's d = 1.17), whereas ferritin remained unchanged and hematological parameters showed no consistent between-group differences.
CONCLUSION: Black chokeberry supplementation may influence markers related to short-term post-exercise iron availability, potentially in association with inflammatory and antioxidant responses, without detectable effects on body iron stores or erythropoiesis.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT06486623; registration date: 2024-07-03).

title: Recovery Kinetics After Particulated Autologous Cartilage With Platelet-Rich Plasma for Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus in Athletes: Functional Scores Track Function but Show Limited Return-to-Sport Prediction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Talar cartilage repair is reported through 12-month endpoints; first-year recovery, a 6-month assessment's predictive value, and sex differences remain unknown.
PURPOSE: To characterize recovery after PACI-PRP for talar osteochondral lesions in athletes and whether 6-month scores predict 12-month function and return to sport (RTS).
METHODS: A secondary analysis of a prospective registry included 50 athletes with talar-dome lesions. FADI (primary), VAS pain, and Karlsson-Petersson scores at baseline, 6, and 12 months were analyzed with the Friedman test and mixed-effects models with a time-by-sex interaction. Front-loading (the share of the 12-month change reached by 6 months), correlation with 12-month scores, and the ROC-curve area (AUC) for RTS were computed.
RESULTS: All outcomes improved (p < 0.001). Recovery was front-loaded, with 67% (FADI), 71% (VAS), and 75% (Karlsson) of the 12-month gain by 6 months. Six-month scores correlated moderately with 12-month function (r = 0.44 to 0.58) but did not usefully discriminate RTS (AUC, 0.41 to 0.61). Early responders (MCID by 6 months) had a higher but non-significant RTS rate than late responders (20/21 vs 21/28; p = 0.115), with comparable 12-month function (86 vs 83; p = 0.242). No significant sex differences were identified (interaction p = 0.234 and 0.070).
CONCLUSIONS: Recovery after PACI-PRP is front-loaded with no significant sex differences. Six-month scores forecast 1-year function moderately and did not usefully predict RTS, indicating that return to play depends on factors beyond joint-specific function - psychological readiness and sport-specific load - warranting prospective study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic study, Level IV.

title: Arthroscopy-Assisted Lower Trapezius Tendon Transfer Provides Superior Midterm Outcomes and Return to Work/Sport Compared With Latissimus Dorsi Tendon Transfer for Irreparable Posterosuperior Rotator Cuff Tears.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare midterm return to work (RTW) and return to sport (RTS) rates, clinical outcomes, muscle strength, and radiologic survivorship between arthroscopy-assisted lower trapezius tendon transfer (aLTT) and arthroscopy-assisted latissimus dorsi tendon transfer (aLDT) in patients with posterosuperior irreparable rotator cuff tears.
METHODS: This retrospective comparative study included patients who underwent aLDT or aLTT for posterosuperior irreparable rotator cuff tears between January 2012 and October 2020, with a minimum follow-up of 5 years. The primary outcomes were RTW and RTS rates. Secondary clinical outcomes included patient-reported outcome measures, active range of motion, and active range of motion strength. Radiological outcomes included acromiohumeral distance and Hamada grade. Graft integrity was assessed using postoperative magnetic resonance imaging. Factors associated with RTW and RTS were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 94 patients were divided into 2 groups according to the surgical procedure: the aLDT group (n = 44) underwent aLDT, and the aLTT group (n = 50) underwent aLTT. The aLTT group showed significantly higher RTW (90.0% vs 72.7%, P = .035) and RTS (88.6% vs 63.3%, P = .020) rates than the aLDT group. Both groups showed significant postoperative improvements in clinical outcomes. Postoperative Constant scores (50.7 ± 11.0 vs 64.8 ± 12.8, P < .001), American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons scores (70.5 ± 10.8 vs 83.8 ± 11.8, P < .001), Activities of Daily Living requiring External Rotation scores (20.6 ± 5.7 vs 25.7 ± 3.9, P < .001), forward elevation (135.7° ± 31.7° vs 153.3° ± 22.5°, P = .005), external rotation at the side (34.1° ± 9.5° vs 54.4° ± 22.9°, P < .001), forward elevation strength (20.4 ± 4.2 N vs 24.5 ± 4.4 N, P < .001), and external rotation strength (19.3 ± 3.7 N vs 23.9 ± 4.8 N, P < .001) were all significantly higher in the aLTT group compared with the aLDT group. The progression of arthritic changes was significantly greater in the aLDT group (50%) compared with the aLTT group (12%) (P < .001). Postoperative forward elevation strength, external rotation strength, and progression of arthritic changes were independently associated with higher odds of RTW and RTS.
CONCLUSIONS: aLTT showed superior RTW and RTS outcomes compared with aLDT at midterm follow-up. These functional advantages were accompanied by greater clinical improvements and more favorable radiologic parameters, reflecting the biomechanical superiority of the aLTT.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Does Smoking Impair Functional Recovery After Total Knee Arthroplasty? A Large-Scale Analysis of Patient-Reported Outcomes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Smoking is a recognized risk factor that adversely affects wound healing, systemic health, and orthopedic outcomes. However, its influence on patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) after total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains insufficiently defined. This study evaluated the association between smoking and postoperative PROMs following primary TKA.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort of 992 patients who underwent primary TKA between January 2020 and January 2023 was analyzed. Patients were categorized as smokers (n = 152, 15.3%) or nonsmokers (n = 840, 84.7%). PROMs included the EQ-5D-5L index, EQ-VAS, and Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) subscales assessing pain, symptoms, activities of daily living, sports/recreation, and quality of life. Outcomes were recorded preoperatively and at 12 months postoperatively. Between-group comparisons were performed using independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests. Multivariate linear regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and baseline PROM scores.
RESULTS: Preoperative PROMs were comparable between smokers and nonsmokers (all p > 0.05). At 12 months, both groups demonstrated significant improvement compared with baseline (all p < 0.001). However, nonsmokers achieved higher postoperative scores than smokers, including EQ-5D-5L (0.82 ± 0.11 vs. 0.75 ± 0.13), EQ-VAS (75.6 ± 14.0 vs. 68.1 ± 15.5), and KOOS quality of life (67.9 ± 15.3 vs. 60.1 ± 16.8) (all p < 0.001). Improvements were also greater among nonsmokers (ΔEQ-VAS p < 0.001). Multivariate analysis confirmed smoking as an independent predictor of worse postoperative PROMs.
CONCLUSIONS: Smoking is an independent risk factor for poorer functional recovery and lower quality of life following primary TKA. These findings may be useful for preoperative patient counseling, indicating that smokers may experience not only an increased risk of postoperative complications, as established in previous studies, but also poorer patient-reported functional outcomes.

title: The role of visual and vestibular disturbances in predicting four-week recovery following acute concussion: a cohort study by sex (from the Toronto concussion study).
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Visual and vestibular disturbances (VVD) are common following concussion, but their relationship with recovery and potential sex differences remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the relationship between early VVD and four-week recovery overall and by sex in community-dwelling adults.
METHODS: This prospective longitudinal study included 122 adults (mean age 36.6 years; 64.6% female) assessed within one week and again four weeks post-concussion. VVD were assessed using the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool-5th Edition (SCAT-5) and a modified Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screen (mVOMS). Recovery was determined by physician evaluation. Logistic regression examined associations between early VVD and recovery while adjusting for injury and sociodemographic covariates.
RESULTS: Male and female participants demonstrated different baseline VVD patterns on the SCAT-5 and mVOMS. At four weeks, 27.9% had recovered. Baseline SCAT-5 visual and vestibular symptoms were not associated with recovery, whereas mVOMS positivity (symptom increase ≥ 4) was associated with non-recovery. No significant sex differences were observed in the association between early VVD and recovery.
CONCLUSIONS: Early mVOMS positivity may have prognostic value for identifying community-dwelling adults at risk of delayed concussion recovery, whereas self-reported visual and vestibular symptoms alone may not. Although early symptom profiles differed by sex, recovery trajectories did not.

title: Effects of neuromuscular electrical stimulation applied simultaneously with exercise therapy in patellofemoral pain: A single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Simultaneous neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) during exercise may augment task-specific quadriceps activation, but its additional effects in patellofemoral pain (PFP) are uncertain. This pilot trial examined whether adding simultaneous NMES improved pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, quadriceps strength, and muscle thickness compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation.
METHODS: In this single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial, 30 participants were allocated 1:1 to an intervention group or acontrol group. Both groups received the same hip- and knee-targeted exercise therapy twice weekly for 6 weeks. The intervention group received NMES during leg press and leg extension exercises, whereas the control group wore the same device with stimulation intensity set to zero. The primary outcome was worst pain during the previous week, assessed using the visual analogue scale(VAS). Secondary outcomes included the anterior knee pain scale (AKPS), Y-Balance Test (YBT) composite score, isokinetic quadriceps strength (60°/s, 180°/s), and quadriceps muscle thickness.
RESULTS: No additional between-group benefit was detected for worst pain (p = .96; Cohen's d = -0.03), AKPS (p = .26; Cohen's d = -0.24), YBT composite (p = .28; Cohen's d = -0.26), isokinetic strength at 60°/s (p = .67; Cohen's d = -0.11), or 180°/s (p = .56; Cohen's d = -0.12). Total quadriceps muscle thickness increased more in the intervention group than in the control group, but the effect was small (p = .03; Cohen's d = -0.27). No adverse events were reported.
CONCLUSION: No additional short-term benefit of adding simultaneous NMES to exercise therapy was detected for pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, or quadriceps strength compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation. A small increase in total quadriceps muscle thickness was detected, but its clinical relevance remains uncertain. These findings do not support routine addition of simultaneous NMES for short-term pain relief or functional improvement.

title: Menstrual Cycle Disorders in Female Athletes: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Objective: Female athletes have a higher prevalence of menstrual disorders due to hormonal imbalances, often related to physical stress, low energy availability, and inadequate nutritional habits. These disorders can affect both health and athletic performance. The aim of this study is to evaluate the frequency of menstrual cycle disorders in female athletes and their relationship with nutritional variables. Design: Observational, descriptive, cross-sectional study based on an anonymous online questionnaire administered to female athletes aged 18-55 years (n = 418; average age = 28 ± 9 years). Methods: The questionnaire collected self-reported data on menstrual cycle characteristics, diet, supplementation, and training-related habits. Chi-square tests, Fisher's exact test, and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used for statistical analysis, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Premenstrual symptoms were reported by 57.0% of participants, regular clot presence by 27.4%, and cycle irregularities by 22.8%. In unadjusted analyses, self-reported dietary balance was associated with cycle regularity and bleeding duration; after false discovery rate correction, only the association with altered bleeding duration (binary coding) remained statistically significant. No clear associations were observed between sports frequency and menstrual cycle alterations. Conclusions: Menstrual disorders were common among female athletes. Although an association between self-reported dietary balance and bleeding duration persisted after correction for multiple comparisons, it derived from an exploratory binary recoding and warrants cautious interpretation. These findings may help guide future research on nutrition and menstrual health in female athletes.

title: Smartphone Accelerometer Assessment of HRV: Concurrent Agreement of the KubiosHRV App.
abstract: Heart rate variability (HRV) is widely used to monitor athlete recovery and adaptation. Recent technological advances have enabled HRV assessment through smartphone applications without the need for external devices. This study aimed to assess the concurrent agreement between the accelerometer-based HRV measurement feature of the KubiosHRV app and the Polar H10 in supine, seated, and standing positions. A total of 52 participants (30 males and 22 females) across performance tiers 0-4 completed a 2 min resting recording, with the first minute discarded and the second minute analysed in each position. HRV was measured simultaneously using a Polar H10 chest strap and the accelerometer-based feature of the KubiosHRV app on an iPhone 14. The analysed variables included Mean RR, RMSSD, SDNN, LF power, HF power, SD1, and SD2. Data were automatically processed by the KubiosHRV app and manually extracted into a database. Results showed excellent intraclass correlation coefficients (≥0.985) and small magnitudes of error for time-domains and non-linear variables in the three analysed positions with the reference criterion. Frequency-domain variables showed larger error estimates. Bland-Altman analysis showed no evidence of proportional bias across the measurement range (p > 0.05). These findings suggest that, during 1 min recordings, the accelerometer-based feature of the KubiosHRV app showed strong concurrent agreement with the Polar H10 for time-domain variables and acceptable agreement for selected non-linear variables across positions. Therefore, it may represent a practical alternative for routine monitoring of these HRV metrics when external hardware is unavailable.

title: The Impact of Race-to-Race Fatigue on Performance in a 24-Hour Competitive Swimming Schedule.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To examine the sequence of physiological, perceptual, and neuromuscular responses to successive competitive events performed within 24 hours in U16 and U18 national-level swimmers and to determine whether cumulative fatigue impairs performance-related markers.
METHODS: Nineteen highly trained junior swimmers (11 males and 8 females; age 16 [1] y) competed in a "direct-final" format (no heats), completing at least 3 separate maximum-effort finals (50-400 m) during the first 24 hours of the Spanish National Championships. Swimmers were categorized by age: U16 and U18. Countermovement jump, blood lactate, heart rate, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were measured 15 minutes before and immediately after each of the 3 events. General linear models and linear mixed-effects models were employed to evaluate the changes over time, group differences (U16 vs U18), sex, and interactions effects. Effect sizes were reported as η2 or partial η2.
RESULTS: Blood lactate concentration increased significantly (P < .001) from prerace to postrace at each event, reaching a peak of 15.4 (4.7) mmol·L-1 in sprinters. U16 swimmers showed a higher cardiovascular response compared with U18 as the competition progressed (P = .002). The swim team achieved a historic sixth-place overall regional finish, with 37% of the athletes improving their personal bests. No sequential reductions were observed for countermovement jump, F(2,16) = 0.54, P = .593, which remained stable at ∼33 to 34 cm postrace for 50 to 100 m and ∼30 to 31 cm for 200- to 400-m finals, indicating preserved neuromuscular performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Although successive races induce substantial metabolic and cardiovascular stress, lower-limb explosive performance remains stable. Youth swimmers appear capable of tolerating congested multievent competition without substantial impairment in lower body neuromuscular power.

title: Systematic Disagreement Between Skinfold-Derived and Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) Body Fat Estimates in Elite Female Trail Runners.
abstract: Background: Converting skinfold thicknesses into body fat percentage (%BF) assumes that subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) represents a fixed fraction of total fat, an assumption untested at extreme leanness. This study assessed whether skinfold-dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) disagreement is random or structured by regional SAT. Methods: Thirty-five elite (Tier 4) female trail runners underwent anthropometry (Withers equation) and DXA in one session. Agreement was evaluated via Bland-Altman analysis and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). The inter-method difference (%BF_GAP = %BF_WITHERS - %BF_DXA) was regressed on android SAT, adjusted for total adiposity, and benchmarked against DXA-derived negative controls. Results: The methods correlated closely (r = 0.866) but showed poor concordance (CCC = 0.311). Skinfold estimates were systematically lower than DXA by 5.50 percentage points (pp; 95% limits of agreement -8.75 to -2.25 pp), with a proportional bias that widened with adiposity. Android SAT was associated with %BF_GAP (R2 = 0.489). Residualized on total fat mass, SAT retained an independent association (ΔR2 = 0.106), which no negative control showed. Propagated skinfold imprecision explained ~1.3% of the difference variance. Conclusions: The methods were not interchangeable. Their disagreement was systematic and associated with android SAT, but the design cannot show which method is closer to true body fat. In comparable athletes, converted skinfold %BF should not be reported alone or compared against DXA reference data; raw skinfold sums are preferable, as a variable to be observed rather than a target to be reduced.

title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain.
METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function).
RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

title: Prospective Polynomial Characterization of Tibial Plateau Geometry Shows No Association With Contralateral ACL Injury in Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are common in athletic people, with young female athletes at particularly high risk. After ACL injury, reconstruction, and return to sport, many sustain contralateral ACL (CACL) injuries. While tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry has been associated with first-time ACL injury risk, its role in subsequent CACL injury remains unclear.
HYPOTHESIS: The normal knee of female athletes who suffered a first-time ACL injury, underwent reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and subsequently suffered a CACL injury will have tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry that is different compared with an equivalent population who did not sustain a subsequent CACL injury.
STUDY DESIGN: Prospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: A total of 199 subjects who suffered a first-time ACL injury, had reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and had a contralateral knee that was normal underwent bilateral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan acquisitions. Tibial plateau cartilage geometry was assessed on the uninjured, normal knees using T1-weighted Fast Field Echo MRI. Parasagittal slices at maximum cartilage concavity in medial and lateral compartments of the tibia were characterized by fitting fifth-order polynomials. Female athletes who sustained a CACL injury within 4 years of reconstruction and return to sport (n = 12) were matched and compared with a group of female athletes who did not sustain CACL injury (n = 24). Random coefficient mixed-effects regression was used to assess group differences in polynomial functions.
RESULTS: No significant differences in tibial cartilage surface geometry were found between the first-time ACL and first-time ACL + CACL injury groups in the medial (P = 0.23) and lateral (P = 0.18) compartments.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that characterization of tibial plateau cartilage geometry in the normal knee of subjects who underwent reconstruction after a first-time ACL injury is insufficient to predict who will on go on to suffer a subsequent CACL injury.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: More comprehensive predictive models incorporating anatomic, biomechanical, and psychological factors are likely needed to identify those at increased risk for CACL injury after a first-time ACL injury and reconstruction.

title: Ischemic Preconditioning Effects in Competitive Swim Athletes: A Randomized Control Trial.
abstract: Montgomery, ME, Scholten, HG, and Scholten, SD. Ischemic preconditioning effects in competitive swim athletes: A randomized control trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Ischemic preconditioning (IPC) has been shown to effectively enhance athletic performance in short-duration (250 yard) swimming, possibly through mechanisms related to the vascular system. Swimming is an ideal mode of exercise to test IPC's effectiveness outside of the lab because of the controlled environment. However, it remains unclear whether these benefits persist over longer swimming distances. To address this gap, this study investigated the potential benefits of IPC on performance in a 500-yard swimming event by conducting a block-randomized controlled trial comparing swim times under 2 IPC conditions: a 1-minute sham condition and a 5-minute IPC intervention. Fourteen NCAA Division II swimmers completed all trials. Eleven out of 14 subjects swam faster (1.72 seconds) with IPC treatment than with sham treatment (p = 0.19; effect size = 0.08). This improvement in time is small, but it is worth considering in competitive sports, where the time difference among competitive athletes is small.

title: Simultaneous versus Staged Bilateral Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Surgical Outcomes and Postoperative Complications.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Knee osteoarthritis commonly presents as a bilateral condition, thereby often indicating the need for bilateral knee arthroplasty to achieve optimal therapeutic outcomes. Simultaneous bilateral knee arthroplasty has emerged as an increasingly favored treatment approach, owing to its numerous clinical advantages. This study aims to compare the clinical outcomes and complications of simultaneous bilateral total knee arthroplasty (sim-BTKA) and staged bilateral total knee arthroplasty (stag-BTKA).
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at Viet Duc University Hospital between November 2021 and March 2024, including 38 patients (12 sim-BTKA and 26 stag-BTKA). All procedures were performed by the same surgeon using a standardized perioperative rehabilitation protocol. Postoperative pain was assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), while functional outcomes were evaluated using the Knee Society Score (KS) and Knee Function Score (KFS). Longitudinal postoperative outcomes were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) to account for repeated measurements over time.
RESULTS: Generalized estimating equation analysis demonstrated significant improvements in VAS, KS, and KFS over time in both groups (all p < 0.001), whereas no significant group-by-time interaction was observed, indicating comparable recovery trajectories between treatment strategies. The simultaneous bilateral total knee arthroplasty (sim-BTKA) procedures were completed in markedly less time, averaging 88.75 minutes versus 104.62 minutes for the staged approach (p = 0.001). While patients undergoing sim-BTKA reported slightly greater postoperative pain based on visual analog scale (VAS) measurements during the first month, and those with staged procedures (stag-BTKA) showed better functional outcomes per Knee Society Scores (KSS) in follow-up assessments, neither trend reached statistical significance (p > 0.05). The average hospital length of stay was significantly shorter in the simultaneous BTKA group compared to the staged BTKA group (9.25 vs. 15.8 days, p = 0.02). Additionally, the total surgical costs were reduced in the simultaneous BTKA cohort ( 2 , 000 v s . 2,760, p = 0.045). No statistically significant differences in postoperative complications were detected between groups; however, the study was not powered to detect small differences in complication rates.
CONCLUSIONS: Simultaneous bilateral total knee arthroplasty (BTKA) reduces operative time, hospital stay, and surgical cost compared to staged BTKA. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in postoperative pain, functional recovery, or complications. However, because of the limited statistical power, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence between treatment strategies. Recommendations: Simultaneous BTKA should be performed in high-capacity orthopedic surgical facilities with experienced surgeons and multidisciplinary perioperative management. Optimal patient selection is essential, prioritizing ASA I-II candidates to reduce surgical risks.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 3 (A retrospective cohort study) Ethical approval: The study was reviewed by the institutional ethics committee, which determined that formal ethical approval was not required because only anonymized retrospective clinical data were analyzed. Funding: The authors received no specific funding for this work.

title: Return to play rate and performance after ulnar collateral ligament repair with suture tape augmentation in major league baseball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) repair with suture tape augmentation has emerged as an alternative to traditional reconstruction in appropriately selected patients. While clinical outcomes of UCL repair have been reported in amateur athletes, data evaluating performance outcomes in Major League Baseball (MLB) players remain limited. The purpose of this study was to evaluate return to play (RTP) and changes in performance metrics among MLB players undergoing UCL repair with suture tape augmentation. We hypothesized that UCL repair would allow a faster RTP compared with historical reconstruction data while maintaining player performance.
METHODS: MLB players who underwent UCL repair with suture tape augmentation between 2016 and 2024 were identified using publicly available injury databases. Player performance metrics were obtained from publicly available databases including MLB Statcast. The primary outcome was time to RTP. Secondary outcomes included traditional and advanced performance metrics. For pitchers, metrics included earned run average, innings pitched, strikeouts, walk rate, fastball velocity, fastball spin rate, fielder independent pitching, fangraphs wins above replacement (fWAR), and Statcast-based metrics. Position player metrics included fWAR, fielding run value, and arm strength. Pre-operative and post-operative metrics were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests or Mann-Whitney tests with statistical significance set at P < .05.
RESULTS: Twenty-two MLB players met inclusion criteria. RTP to the MLB level was 81.8% (18/22). The mean RTP time was 10.98 months (range, 5.9-34). Pitchers had a mean RTP of 13.51 months (range, 9-34) and position players had a mean RTP of 7.51 months (range, 5.9-8.5). There were no statistically significant differences between pre-operative and post-operative performance metrics, including earned run average (3.66 ± 0.7 vs. 3.95 ± 1.9; P = .765), fastball velocity (93.0 ± 1.7 vs. 92.7 ± 1.9 mph; P = .609), innings pitched (42.1 ± 39.0 vs. 23.0 ± 28.0; P = .266), strikeouts (31.7 ± 53.7 vs. 23.5 ± 27.4; P = .247), or fastball spin rate (2,241 ± 131 vs. 2,235 ± 122 rpm; P = .496). Similarly, position players demonstrated no significant differences in fWAR, fielding run value, or arm strength after RTP.
CONCLUSION: UCL repair with suture tape augmentation in MLB players demonstrates a high rate of RTP with preservation of traditional and advanced performance metrics. Position players returned earlier than pitchers; overall RTP remained favorable. UCL repair with suture tape augmentation provides an effective surgical option allowing return to elite-level performance.
