title: Ramp lesions repaired during anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction are associated with similar functional outcomes to other medial meniscal lesions at 1 year: A prospective registry-based study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate 12-month outcomes after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) in patients with repaired ramp lesions compared with patients with other medial meniscal lesions or no meniscal lesions.
METHODS: This prospective registry-based study included patients undergoing primary ACLR with 12-month follow-up. Three propensity-score-matched comparisons were performed: ramp versus other medial meniscal lesions (94 vs. 94), ramp versus no meniscal lesions (107 vs. 205), and other medial meniscal lesions versus no meniscal lesions (103 vs. 103). Outcomes included knee function, psychological readiness, satisfaction and return to sport and work. Patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) and minimal clinically important difference (MCID) were defined as International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores ≥75.9 and improvements ≥10.7 points, respectively.
RESULTS: Among 110 patients with ramp lesions (60.9% male; mean age, 25.9 ± 8.9 years), knee function improved significantly at 12 months (p < 0.001). Postoperative IKDC scores did not differ significantly between ramp lesions and other medial meniscal lesions (86.6 vs. 84.5; p = 0.83) or no meniscal lesions (86.6 vs. 87.6; p = 0.15). However, compared with patients without meniscal lesions, those with ramp lesions reported lower subjective knee values (85.0 vs. 90.0; p = 0.007), psychological readiness (67.0 vs. 76.5; p = 0.02) and satisfaction (77.6% vs. 89.3%; p = 0.009). No significant differences were observed between other medial meniscal lesions and no meniscal lesions.
CONCLUSIONS: Repaired ramp lesions were associated with comparable functional outcomes but lower psychological readiness and satisfaction compared with isolated ACLR at 12 months, emphasizing the importance of patient-perceived recovery.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Heart rate variability in police research: a scoping review of objective psychophysiological assessment.
abstract: Policing places substantial psychological and physiological demands on officers, increasing the risk of adverse health outcomes and impaired performance. As wearable physiological sensing technologies have become more accessible, heart rate variability (HRV) has emerged as a widely used measure of autonomic and psychophysiological regulation. This scoping review synthesized the application of HRV in policing research and identified methodological considerations and future directions. PubMed, Web of Science, MEDLINE, and PsycINFO were systematically searched for primary studies involving police personnel that used HRV as a measure or outcome. Following screening and full-text review, 58 studies comprising 4,764 participants were included. A narrative synthesis identified three broad applications of HRV: (1) health and well-being, (2) stress response and performance, and (3) adaptive regulation. Lower HRV was consistently associated with occupational stress, shift work, poorer recovery, obesity, and metabolic dysfunction, whereas greater physical activity, aerobic fitness, and healthier body composition were associated with more adaptive autonomic profiles facilitating recovery from stress. During acute operational demands, reductions in vagally mediated HRV and greater sympathetic activation were generally associated with poorer performance, while broader HRV measures were linked to fatigue, tactical selection, and operational readiness. Breathing-based interventions, such as HRV biofeedback and mindfulness were associated with improvements in autonomic regulation, recovery, training adaptation, and performance. Despite these encouraging findings, substantial conceptual and methodological heterogeneity limited interpretation of the evidence. As a scoping review, the objective was to characterize the breadth of HRV applications in policing rather than estimate pooled effects. Accordingly, studies were included across diverse designs and HRV applications. HRV was used as an indicator of stress, recovery, autonomic regulation, health, and performance, with marked variation in theoretical frameworks, HRV metrics, sensing technologies, recording protocols, and outcome measures. Collectively, the findings demonstrate that HRV is a feasible objective measure in policing research. Future work should prioritize theory-driven study designs, standardized measurement, reporting, and methodological controls to strengthen objective inference from physiological sensing. Currently, HRV should be interpreted as one component of a broader psychophysiological assessment. It should not be used for personnel selection, fitness-for-duty, or prediction of mental health.

title: Thumb muscle activation with task-specific exercise: A pilot study with participant self-report implementation outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis is a common source of pain, weakness, and reduced hand function and upper extremity rehabilitation. Although isometric stabilization exercises are commonly used in hand therapy to support dynamic thumb carpometacarpal control, limited task-specific evidence guides exercise selection.
PURPOSE: To examine muscle activation across four isometric thumb-hand positions in healthy adults and describe participant perceptions of the protocol's acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness before testing in symptomatic hand therapy samples.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional, within-subject repeated-measures pilot study.
METHODS: Seven healthy right-handed adults (mean age, 22.7 ± 0.48 years) performed four submaximal isometric exercise conditions at approximately 80% perceived effort: composite finger-thumb squeeze, "bunny-ears" pinch, resisted index-finger abduction, and fingertip-only press. Surface electromyography was recorded from the abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, first dorsal interosseous, and forearm flexor group. Integrated electromyography was normalized within participants to each muscle's maximum response across conditions. A two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (condition × muscle) compared normalized activation. Participants rated acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness on five-point Likert scales.
RESULTS: Normalized activation differed by muscle, F(3,18) = 14.22, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.70, with a significant condition × muscle interaction, F(9,54) = 7.29, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.55. Abductor pollicis brevis activation was highest during composite squeeze and bunny-ears pinch (0.93 ± 0.05 and 0.85 ± 0.06) and lowest during resisted index-finger abduction (0.31 ± 0.07). Opponens pollicis activation was highest during composite squeeze and resisted index-finger abduction (0.79 ± 0.07 and 0.75 ± 0.09). Mean construct-based ratings of acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness ranged from 4.54-4.79 out of 5.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings provide preliminary evidence to inform hand therapy exercise selection by showing that functional isometric thumb-hand positions produce distinct intrinsic and extrinsic activation profiles. Favorable participant perceptions support protocol refinement and testing in larger and symptomatic hand therapy samples.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Immediate Effects of Kinesiotaping on Lower Limb Biomechanics and Interlimb Symmetry in Return-to-Sport Athletes After ACL Reconstruction.
abstract: Residual biomechanical deficits may persist during landing after ACL reconstruction despite meeting return-to-sport criteria, and the immediate effects of kinesiotaping (KT) remain unclear. This study investigated bilateral lower limb biomechanics and the immediate effects of KT in 18 return-to-sport athletes after ACL reconstruction. Three-dimensional motion capture and dual force plates were used during the landing absorption phase. Statistical parametric mapping and 2-way repeated-measures analysis of variance were applied for analysis, and the limb symmetry index was calculated to assess interlimb symmetry. The uninvolved limb demonstrated greater vertical ground reaction force, loading rate, knee and ankle joint work (P < .05), hip external rotation moment (P = .025), and knee flexion moment (P < .001) than the involved limb. KT reduced knee varus and external rotation angles and internal knee valgus moment in the involved limb (P < .05) and increased bilateral hip work contribution (P = .026). However, KT did not significantly improve interlimb symmetry (P > .05). ACL reconstruction athletes meeting return-to-sport criteria continue to exhibit bilateral biomechanical asymmetries during landing. KT improved frontal- and transverse-plane knee control and promoted a more proximal energy absorption strategy, but restoring interlimb symmetry requires comprehensive neuromuscular rehabilitation.

title: Time-Efficient Reactive Agility Training Improves Motor and Cognitive Components of Reactive Agility in Open- and Closed-Skill Athletes: A 6-Week Intervention Study.
abstract: Reactive agility (RA), the ability to respond to external stimuli with whole-body movements as quickly and precisely as possible, is crucial for many sports, particularly open-skill sports, and is influenced by both motor and cognitive abilities. This study aims to investigate which of the underlying components of RA is most improved through RA training, whether prior experience with RA movements influences the rate of improvement, and whether a time-ecological approach also leads to improvements. Assessments included 19 open-skill and 26 closed-skill athletes with different competitive backgrounds. RA training was carried out once a week for six weeks with each session lasting 20 minutes. Pre- and post-assessments were conducted for RA (Random Star Run), change-of-direction (t-Test), and cognitive performance (Stroop test). Baseline differences between open- and closed-skill athletes and performance level were evaluated using 2 × 2 ANOVA. Intervention effects were calculated using repeated measures ANOVA. Open-skill athletes were significantly faster within the RA task than closed-skill athletes (p = 0.017; F = 6.247; η2 p = 0.132). Both groups improved significantly across all outcome measures (p < 0.05; RA and both underlying properties) with no interaction effects of group × time (p > 0.05). One weekly 20-min training session is sufficient to improve RA, and selected motor and cognitive performance parameters. Prior experience, based on regular participation in open-skill sports, seems to be associated with higher RA performance but does not moderate training adaptations, as both groups improved similarly in RA and the underlying motor and cognitive functions.

title: Sex- and Sport-Specific Differences in Mobility and Muscle Function Characteristics in Division I Athletes.
abstract: Gonzalez, AM, Sell, KM, Mangine, GT, Ghigiarelli, JJ, Gerland, RW, Deveaux, B, DiMonda, R, Prendergast, JM, and Bentivegna, J. Sex- and sport-specific differences in mobility and muscle function characteristics in Division I athletes. J Strength Cond Res 40(12): 1569-1580, 2026-The purpose of the present investigation was to compare sex- and sport-specific differences in joint mobility, bilateral asymmetry, and muscle function characteristics among Division I collegiate athletes. Two hundred and seventy six male (n = 144) and female (n = 132) athletes from 7 sports completed a comprehensive, preseason assessment battery. Mobility assessments included hip, shoulder, ankle, thoracic, and pelvic range-of-motion, as well as sit-and-reach performance. Muscle function assessments included measures of vertical jump height, hand grip strength, and hip abduction/adduction strength. Measures were analyzed using mixed-model analyses of variance to examine effects of sex, sport, and limb dominance. Clear sex- and sport-specific differences were observed across multiple mobility measures. Female athletes demonstrated significantly greater joint mobility than male athletes across several anatomical regions (p < 0.001-0.03; η2p = 0.02-0.16), whereas male athletes display superior muscle function performance across strength (p < 0.001-0.02; η2p = 0.06-0.3) and vertical jump (p < 0.001, η2p = 0.50) measures. Mobility asymmetries varied substantially by sport and joint, while strength asymmetries were minimal across groups. These findings provide sex- and sport-specific reference data and reinforce the importance of individualized interpretation of mobility and muscle function assessments in athletic populations.

title: Age-related slowing of sensorimotor reaction time in masters track and field athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Masters athletes offer a powerful model for understanding how lifelong training shapes age‑related changes in reaction time (RT), a key indicator of sensorimotor performance.
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional study examined RT in masters track and field athletes across age, sex, RT tasks of varying complexity, and event disciplines (endurance, power, sprint).
METHODS: A total of 182 competitors (82 females) from the 2025 World Masters Athletics Championships completed four RT tasks using a wireless light-based testing system.
RESULTS: RT increased progressively with age across all tasks, with the slowest responses consistently observed in athletes ≥80 years old. Female athletes demonstrated slower RT than males, and RT increased systematically with task complexity. Sprint athletes showed faster RT than endurance athletes overall, although event‑specific differences did not persist within age groups. Age was positively associated with RT in all tasks (r = 0.41-0.53), with similar correlation strengths between sexes. Quadratic age effects emerged selectively in male athletes for two-hand simple and step-choice tasks, suggesting accelerated slowing at older ages in tasks requiring greater motor coordination. Linear regression models indicated that RT increased by approximately 3.3-3.6 ms per year of age after adjusting for sex, task, and event discipline, while body composition variables were not significant predictors.
CONCLUSIONS: Although lifelong training is associated with better sensorimotor performance, slower RT remains evident in masters athletes, with consistent sex differences and minimal influence of event discipline.

title: Enhancing Sleep in NCAA Division I Athletes: A Study of Sleep Extension Feasibility.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep extension has been shown to improve varied aspects of athletic performance in collegiate athletes. Such studies have been conducted in small cohorts in controlled settings utilizing obsolete monitoring technology. The feasibility of sleep extension has not been evaluated in a broader cohort of collegiate athletes with modern monitoring technology.
HYPOTHESIS: Sleep extension may not be feasible in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Baseline sleep data were collected from NCAA Division I athletes (women's soccer, men's soccer, baseball, and football) during a 2-week period. Subjects were then instructed to extend their total sleep time to 10 hours per night for 2 weeks. All sleep baseline and extension data were collected in the offseason, remote from school examinations. WHOOP bands recorded all sleep metrics. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests.
RESULTS: A total of 50 subjects (14 female, 36 male) participated. The study compared total sleep time (hours) and sleep consistency (percent) - the stability of sleep-wake schedule over time, between baseline and sleep extension phases. Sample size varied for both metrics, ranging from 46 to 49 participants, respectively. There was a statistically significant increase in sleep consistency during the sleep extension phase (baseline, 60.09 ± 12.6%; extension, 64.42 ± 12.4%; P = 0.02). However, total sleep time showed no significant difference between the 2 phases (baseline, 7.63 ± 0.88 hours; extension, 7.51 ± 0.88 hours; P = 0.27).
CONCLUSION: Extension efforts improved sleep consistency but did not significantly impact total sleep time suggesting that a sleep extension intervention can enhance sleep consistency in NCAA Division I athletes but does not significantly impact total sleep time. Sleep extension may be challenging for collegiate athletes given the time-intensive demands of both academics and sports. While sleep extension may be feasible in professional sports, it does not appear to be so in the college setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the sleep extension intervention improved sleep consistency, it did not improve total sleep time, questioning the feasibility of sleep extension in collegiate sports.

title: The Relationship Between Muscle Strength and Jump Height with Bone Mineral Density (BMD) in Elite Female Soccer Players: The Mediating Role of Lean Body Mass.
abstract: Soccer is one of the most widely practiced and studied sports worldwide. The increasing professionalization of women's soccer has raised interest in bone health. This study aimed to analyze the mediating role of lean body mass in the association between muscle strength, jump height, and bone mineral density (BMD) in elite female soccer players. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 28 players from the Spanish national soccer team. Muscle strength was assessed using estimated 1RM in the deadlift, jump height through the countermovement jump (CMJ) test, and BMD using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Lean body mass exhibited a significant indirect effect on the association between muscle strength and BMD at the lumbar spine (β = 0.2848, B = 0.0020, 95% CI for B [0.0001-0.0049]), femoral neck (β = 0.2562, B = 0.0020, 95% CI for B [0.0003-0.0052]), and whole body (β = 0.3769, B = 0.0019, 95% CI for B [0.0005-0.0038]). These results suggest that muscle strength alone may not fully explain inter-individual differences in bone mass and that lean body mass may play an important role in this relationship. Combining soccer training with targeted strength training could help maximize peak bone mass and mitigate future bone loss in these female athletes. Longitudinal studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Immediate Return or Overnight Stay? Sleep Responses by Postmatch Travel Strategy and Match Participation in Professional Football.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Late European away fixtures can disrupt sleep, but the influence of immediate return versus overnight stay, and whether responses differ by match participation, remains unclear.
HYPOTHESIS: Postmatch travel strategy would influence sleep quality and duration across the prematch, match, and subsequent nights, with responses moderated by match participation.
STUDY DESIGN: Observational repeated-measures field study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: A total of 19 outfield English Premier League players were monitored across 10 European away fixtures (5 immediate return and 5 overnight stay). Self-reported sleep quality (1 to 7) and sleep duration were recorded on the prematch, match, and subsequent nights. Fixed-effects models examined condition, time, and match participation, with standard errors clustered by player.
RESULTS: Sleep quality was lower than prematch baseline on the match and subsequent nights (both β = -0.62 arbitrary units [AU]; P < 0.01; g = -0.63). After overnight stay, sleep quality improved from the match to the subsequent night in players who participated and those who did not (β = 0.69 and 0.63 AU; 95% CIs, 0.37-0.90 and 0.47-0.91; P < 0.01), whereas no change occurred after immediate return. Across participation groups, sleep duration was lower after overnight stay than immediate return on the match night (β = -1.94 hours; P < 0.01; g = -1.26) and subsequent night (β = -1.02 hours; P = 0.02; g = -0.67). However, after overnight stay, sleep duration increased between these nights by 1.45 hours in participants and 1.43 hours in nonparticipants (P < 0.01), with no significant change after immediate return. Participation moderated sleep duration on both postfixture nights (β = 1.27 and 1.64 hours; P ≤ 0.04; g = 0.82 and 1.07).
CONCLUSION: Neither travel strategy was uniformly superior. Overnight stay was associated with poorer absolute sleep duration but a clearer next-night rebound in sleep quality and duration.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Postmatch travel should be planned case by case, considering itinerary, next-day demands, and individual match exposure rather than applying a single team-wide policy.

title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
abstract: Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

title: Bone Health in Female Athletes Using Hormonal Contraceptives.
abstract: The objectives of this study were to (1) report the prevalence and type of hormonal contraception (HC) use among Canadian elite and world-class athletes and (2) investigate associations between current HC use and bone density, microarchitecture and strength, accounting for sport type (endurance vs. non-endurance). Participants included 61 high performance athletes, mean age 24 years. Endurance-based sport affiliations include long-track speed skating (n=16), cross-country skiing (n=13) and biathlon (n=9). Non-endurance sports were ski cross (n=7), figure skating (n=6), luge (n=4), ski jumping (n=4), and combat sports (n=2). High-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography scans of the radius and tibia were acquired and outcome measures included bone mineral density, microarchitecture, geometry and bone strength. Questionnaires captured sport affiliation and reproductive health information. Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to examine the effects of current HC use (yes/no) and sport type (endurance/non-endurance) on bone variables. HC prevalence was 69% (n=42) and the majority of athletes used progestin only intrauterine devices (IUDs, n=29). No evidence of detrimental effects resulting from HC use was found in this cohort. Although some differences were observed between groups, no interaction effects remained significant after multiple-comparison correction and these findings should be interpreted with caution. Overall, the results do not support clinically meaningful differences in bone health between HC groups. These findings highlight the need for longitudinal research examining the effects of currently prevalent HC methods, particularly IUDs, on overall bone health and strength along with lifetime fracture risk in athletes.

title: Microcurrent Neuromodulation and Stress-Recovery Markers Across a Competitive Season in Elite Female Soccer Athletes: A Controlled Pilot Study.
abstract: Background: Elite women's soccer involves sustained physical and psychosocial demands that may affect endocrine regulation, autonomic recovery, and sleep across the competitive season. Non-invasive neuromodulation has been proposed as an adjunct recovery strategy; however, longitudinal in-season evidence in elite female athletes remains limited. Methods: This controlled pilot trial included 12 elite female soccer players (mean age of 21.4 ± 5.2 years), allocated in a 1:1 ratio to a NESA intervention group (n = 6) or a no-intervention control group (n = 6). The intervention consisted of 32 sessions delivered over eight weeks, with four sessions per week and no sessions on match days. Outcomes were assessed at five predefined time points across the competitive season. Primary physiological outcomes were salivary cortisol and heart rate variability (HRV), complemented by subjective sleep quality (PSQI), competitive state anxiety (CSAI-2), and menstruation-related quality of life (CVM-22). Results: All participants completed the protocol, and no adverse events were reported. The main finding was observed at the post-intervention assessment (M4), where salivary cortisol concentrations were significantly lower in the NESA group than in the control group (7.62 ± 4.02 vs. 25.90 ± 9.92 µg/dL; independent Student's t-test, t = -4.184, df = 10, p = 0.002). Subjective sleep quality showed divergent descriptive trajectories during the pre-post intervention interval: PSQI scores decreased in the NESA group from M3 to M4 and increased in the control group, although the between-group comparison of change was not statistically significant (p = 0.183). Continuous HRV indices did not show a consistent pattern favouring the NESA group; however, categorical HRV profiles suggested descriptive maintenance of a high HRV classification in the intervention group. No consistent intervention-related effects were observed for competitive state anxiety or menstruation-related quality of life. Conclusions: In this controlled pilot study, an eight-week NESA non-invasive neuromodulation protocol was associated with lower post-intervention salivary cortisol concentrations in elite female soccer players. Sleep and HRV findings should be interpreted as complementary descriptive signals, whereas anxiety and menstruation-related quality of life did not show consistent intervention-related changes. Given the small sample size, open-label design, absence of a sham control, and unadjusted baseline differences in cortisol concentrations and sleep quality between groups, these findings should be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Larger, adequately powered, sham-controlled trials are needed to determine the magnitude, specificity, and practical relevance of these findings.

title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

title: Platelet Concentrates in Tooth Replantation: A Narrative Review and Evidence Synthesis of Periodontal and Pulpal Healing.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The prognosis of an avulsed, replanted tooth over the long term hinges on whether the periodontal ligament (PDL) and the dental pulp can be preserved or regenerated. When extra-oral dry time is prolonged, PDL necrosis follows, and the root becomes prone to inflammatory or replacement (ankylotic) resorption. Platelet concentrates-platelet-rich plasma (PRP), leukocyte- and platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP), and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF)-are autologous biomaterials that supply growth factors and may influence this healing process. This review asks whether autologous platelet concentrates reduce inflammatory and replacement (ankylotic) root resorption and improve periodontal and pulpal healing after delayed or intentional tooth replantation, compared with no adjunct, and whether residual periodontal ligament (PDL) viability changes this effect.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This narrative synthesis (not a systematic review) draws together recent controlled clinical and animal studies with the case-report and preclinical literature already captured in the only published systematic review on this topic. The search covered PubMed, Google Scholar, the Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, from January to May 2026.
RESULTS: In preclinical models, L-PRP and PRF promote pulpal repair, tertiary dentin formation, and attenuated inflammatory root resorption, although neither consistently prevents ankylosis once PDL viability has been lost. In one retrospective comparative study of intentional replantation in hopeless teeth, PRF combined with root-surface biomodification produced greater clinical attachment gain and a larger reduction in probing depth than replantation alone, a direction consistent with earlier case reports. Small, largely non-randomized samples and unstandardized protocols still limit this evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Platelet concentrates are biologically plausible adjuncts that improve periodontal and pulpal healing indices, yet they do not reliably prevent ankylosis. Their clinical role will remain undefined until prospective randomized trials with standardized protocols are available.

title: Return to Sport Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Martial Arts and Combat Sports: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physical demands in martial arts and combat sports put substantial stress on the knee, particularly the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). ACL injuries are highly debilitating in these sports, yet return-to-sport (RTS) data remains sparse.
PURPOSE: We sought to investigate: (1) What are the RTS rates and timelines for combat athletes following ACL reconstruction (ACLR)? (2) How does ACLR impact post-operative performance metrics? (3) What is the risk profile for subsequent ACL injury?
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review of PubMed, Scopus, Embase, SPORTDiscus, and Google Scholar through February 22, 2026, for clinical studies reporting RTS, performance, or secondary injury metrics following ACLR in martial arts and combat sport athletes.
RESULTS: Six studies met the inclusion criteria (338 total ACLRs). Initial RTS rates to any participation were high (76.9%-86.3%), but durable return was less consistent when using stricter endpoints, such as Ultimate Fighting Championship sustained return (≥2 fights: 56.3%) or return to preinjury competitive levels (57.7%). One professional fighter study reported a significant postoperative decline, including a reduction in strike evasion among these athletes. Among studies reporting secondary ACL injury or subsequent ACL surgery, rates ranged from 13.1% to 20.0%. Fear of reinjury was a notable psychological barrier to return.
CONCLUSION: The findings of this systematic review of Level-III and Level-IV studies suggest that return to training for combat athletes after ACLR is achievable, but durable return to elite or preinjury competition is less consistently demonstrated and carries substantial secondary injury risk.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV: systematic review of Level-III and Level-IV studies.

title: Monitoring External Load and Internal Responses Across Selected Endurance Sports: A Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Endurance-sport monitoring combines external-load measures with physiological and subjective responses, but studies vary in their measurement techniques, interpretation, and links to action. This scoping review mapped how these indicators have been studied and the types of evidence linking them to training and athlete outcomes.
METHODS: PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched on 24 October 2026. Eligible original research evaluated at least one non-invasive indicator on at least two days during a documented training period or endurance exposure of seven days or longer in six selected endurance sports. Age eligibility was a sample mean/median of at least 18 years or explicit adult recruitment. Findings were summarized descriptively without meta-analysis or formal critical appraisal.
RESULTS: Of 8398 screened records, 83 database-derived reports and six reports from other methods were assessed in full, and 56 reports were included. Of these, 15 reports concerned training-load quantification, 32 examined autonomic or physiological responses, and 9 studied subjective responses. By evidence type, 13 examined measurement properties or response behavior, 20 considered concurrent or longitudinal associations, 12 assessed prospective relationships, and 11 examined monitoring-informed action rules. Relationships varied with calibration, measurement protocol, time window, sport, and outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: The mapped comparisons do not establish broad transferable action thresholds or comparative effectiveness. Future research should evaluate explicit monitoring-and-action rules against adaptations, performance, and health outcomes.

title: Paraspinal Muscle Quality and Functional Outcomes Following Lumbar Fusion: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) procedures are associated with postoperative paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (FI), which may influence long-term pain and functional recovery. However, the relationship between muscle quality, both pre- and postoperatively, and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear for patients undergoing lumbar fusion. This correlation was compared between minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and conventional open surgery (COS) approaches to assess differences in postoperative muscle preservation and functional outcomes.
METHODS: A systematic review, conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250650064), examined studies found in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through February 2025. Studies were included if they assessed adult patients undergoing LIF with preoperative CT or MRI evaluation of the multifidus (MF) or erector spinae (ES) and reported postoperative cross-sectional area (CSA), FI, or patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for 19 non-randomized studies and RoB 2 for one randomized trial. Seven of nine COS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, including all three COS-only studies, measured by CSA and FI. Two of twelve MIS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, with four of six direct comparisons found smaller declines in CSA, increases in FI, or both after MIS compared to COS in at least one muscle or setting. Higher preoperative muscle quality, particularly lower FI, and smaller pre- to postoperative muscle changes were associated with greater PROM improvements. Across the PROM-focused studies, four of the five reported that higher preoperative CSA or lower FI predicted better postoperative improvements in functional outcomes, with one identifying that MF FI of 61% or greater as a threshold for failing to achieve clinically meaningful ODI improvements.
CONCLUSION: MIS techniques were associated with a decrease in pre- to postoperative FI compared with COS, although PROM improvement occurred across both approaches. While preoperative paraspinal muscle quality and size decreases are generally smaller with better functional outcomes following postoperative LIF, this relationship is not consistently observed across all studies or surgical techniques. These findings suggest that the current imaging-based biomarkers may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of functional recovery and underscore the need for further research into additional predictors of muscle recovery.

title: Anthocyanin-Rich Aronia melanocarpa Supplementation Modulates Intestinal Barrier Biomarkers and Stress-Axis Response in a Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anthocyanin-rich berries may modulate intestinal barrier-related processes and physiological stress responses, but evidence from human studies remains limited.
METHODS: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 15 elite male rowers (Aronia group, n = 7; placebo group, n = 8). Participants received Aronia melanocarpa supplementation or placebo for eight weeks and performed a standardized 2000-m rowing ergometer test before and after the intervention. Circulating claudin-3 (CLDN-3), lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP), intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP), and cortisol concentrations were assessed before exercise, immediately after exercise, and following 1 h of recovery.
RESULTS: A significant Group × Time interaction was observed for CLDN-3 (p = 0.0463). After eight weeks, pre-exercise CLDN-3 concentrations were lower in the Aronia group than in the placebo group (p = 0.0367). Lower pre-exercise LBP concentrations (p = 0.0125) and lower cortisol concentrations at 1 h post-exercise (p = 0.0079) were also observed in the Aronia group compared with placebo. No significant supplementation-specific effect was observed for I-FABP.
CONCLUSIONS: Eight weeks of Aronia melanocarpa supplementation was associated with differences in selected intestinal barrier-related biomarkers and post-exercise cortisol concentrations in elite male rowers. However, these findings were primarily related to specific sampling time points and should not be interpreted as evidence of improved intestinal barrier function. Given the small sample size and potential dietary confounding, the results are preliminary and require confirmation in larger randomized controlled trials.

title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.
METHODS: Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.
RESULTS: Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.
CONCLUSIONS: The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach.
STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing.
RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria.
DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions.
CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Low energy availability in recreational high-intensity functional training athletes: associations with health and performance outcomes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Low energy availability (LEA) is the primary etiological factor underlying Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), yet limited research has examined LEA risk and associated health and performance outcomes in recreational high-intensity functional training (HIFT) athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate energy availability (EA) and physiological outcomes aligned with the RED-S Health and Performance Models in a recreational HIFT cohort.
METHODS: Thirty participants (females: n = 18, males: n = 12; 31.2 ± 8.2 years) completed a two-week prospective observational study with repeated measures of energy intake, exercise energy expenditure, and associated health and performance-related measures. Energy intake was assessed via dietary logs, exercise energy expenditure was estimated using a wearable armband, and EA was calculated relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived fat-free mass. Participants were classified as LEA if EA was <30 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1. Performance-related outcomes included rating of perceived exertion (RPE), perceived recovery status (PRS), and total quality recovery (TQR). Health-related outcomes included sleep duration, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and bone mineral density (BMD) (reported by Z-Score).
RESULTS: Mean EA was 24.9 ± 9.7 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1, with 80% (n = 24) of participants demonstrating EA below the LEA classification threshold. The high prevalence of LEA should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for underreporting dietary intake. LEA status was not associated with differences in recovery, sleep quality, or BMD (p > 0.05), and EA was not significantly correlated with performance or health outcomes. In an exploratory analysis, sleep duration was moderately positively associated with TQR (ρ = 0.46, p = 0.01); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the number of comparisons performed.
DISCUSSION: Despite the high prevalence of LEA, associated health and performance impairments were not detected, suggesting that measurable consequences of LEA may not be evident over a short observation period in recreational HIFT athletes. These findings support ongoing monitoring of EA, fueling practices, and recovery behaviors to reduce the potential long-term consequences associated with RED-S.

title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included.
RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed.
CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

title: Force and Power Testing in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Literature: A Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Force and power testing has been recognised as a key aspect of anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) rehabilitation. However, a literature synthesis is required to examine how these physical characteristics have been assessed due to pronounced heterogeneity in the methods used.
OBJECTIVES: To synthesise and describe the existing literature on force and power testing post-ACLR.
METHODS: A scoping review of the electronic databases MEDLINE (PubMed), SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library and PEDro was conducted including studies adopting at least one force or power test in patients post-ACLR. The search methodology followed the Joanna Briggs Institute Manual for evidence synthesis and included the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR).
RESULTS: In total, 1625 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria. Seven main device categories were identified, with different rates of implementation over the years (1981-2023) and throughout the recovery process: (1) isokinetic dynamometry (IKD; 64.9%), (2) jump (without force platform; 32.2%), (3) force platform (28.0%), (4) traditional gym equipment and bodyweight exercises (6.2%), (5) hand-held dynamometry (4.0%), (6) manual muscle testing (1.5%) and (7) other devices (5.5%). Studies used 1.42 ± 0.62 devices, with 45 different combinations recorded. Various tests were conducted using different devices, ranging from 8 to 72 recorded tests per category. Only force plate assessments showed a linear increment in implementation from the surgical procedure (r = 0.86, p = 0.012).
CONCLUSIONS: Significant heterogeneity in assessment device selection, metrics analysed, test implementation and protocols was observed. Most studies included a single device category to examine force and power characteristics of patients post-ACLR. The IKD remains the most adopted testing device in research, but current assessment practices are more varied than in the past.

title: Home-based transcranial direct current stimulation and exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis: A mixed-methods pilot randomised controlled trial.
abstract: This mixed-methods pilot trial evaluated the feasibility and patient perceptions of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. Twenty-four participants were allocated to active or sham home-based tDCS plus exercise. Participants completed 10 tDCS sessions over two weeks and an eight-week exercise program, with laboratory assessments at baseline, week four, and week eight. Primary outcomes were recruitment, adherence, adverse events, attrition, and tolerability. Secondary outcomes included local pressure pain thresholds, pain, function, quality of life, and semi-structured interviews exploring intervention facilitators and barriers. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively and qualitative data using inductive thematic analysis. All prespecified feasibility and safety criteria were met. Adherence was high, with 88% of participants (21/24) completing at least 75% of tDCS sessions, and 75% (18/24) completing at least 75% of exercise sessions. No significant adverse events occurred. Mean (SD) pain intensity /100 decreased from 47.3 (25.6) to 28.3 (16.1) in the active group and from 46.4 (17.8) to 33.5 (16.7) in the sham group at week 8. A future trial would require 80 participants. Qualitative themes indicated that evidence of effectiveness was more important to engagement than financial cost, tDCS was viewed as an appealing alternative to pharmacological treatment, and initial device operation was a greater barrier than safety or home use. Home-based tDCS combined with exercise was feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable intervention improves pain and function in people with knee osteoarthritis. PERSPECTIVE: This pilot trial indicates that home-based tDCS combined with exercise is feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated for knee osteoarthritis. Participants valued its convenience and non-pharmacological nature. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable approach improves pain and function and broadens access to care.

title: Acute Effects of Two Warm-Up Protocols on Sprint Interval Swimming Performance and Physiological Responses in Trained Athletes: Implications for Swimming Training Practice.
abstract: This study examined the acute effects of two practice-based warm-up (WU) protocols on sprint interval swimming performance, physiological and perceptual responses, and stroke characteristics. Fifteen competitive swimmers (World Aquatic Points: 611.2) completed two randomized sessions. Following a 1200 m general WU, swimmers performed either a critical-speed protocol (CSp; 8 × 50 m) or a sprint-interval protocol (SIp; 4 × 15 m maximal efforts). After 4 min passive recovery, swimmers completed a main interval set (MIS; 2 × 4 × 25 m maximal swims). Muscle oxygen saturation (SmO2), heart rate (HR), blood lactate concentration (BLa), and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were recorded at three testing points. Swimming time, fatigue index (FI), velocity decrement (Vdec), and total stroke count (TS) were assessed during the MIS. No significant protocol main effect was detected for MIS time, FI, Vdec, SmO2, or HR; however, MIS time showed a protocol × set interaction (p = 0.024), and TS was higher following SIp (p = 0.025). BLa values across testing points were 3.80 ± 1.61, 8.17 ± 2.39, and 10.53 ± 3.64 mmol·L-1 following CSp, and 4.20 ± 1.45, 11.61 ± 2.60, and 12.77 ± 2.48 mmol·L-1 following SIp (time and protocol effects: p < 0.001; protocol × time interaction: p = 0.006). RPE was higher following SIp (p < 0.05). The protocols elicited different metabolic and perceptual responses and performance trajectories across sets, without a significant overall protocol effect on swimming time. Coaches may select WU configurations according to the intended metabolic and perceptual stimuli.

title: Association Between Collision Exposure and Post-Match Physiological Recovery Markers in Rugby Union Players: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background: Collision exposure during rugby union matches may influence post-match fatigue and recovery. However, direct evidence linking quantified match-related collision exposure to post-match recovery outcomes is limited. Objective: To systematically review associations between match-related collision exposure and post-match recovery outcomes in rugby union players and distinguish direct evidence from indirect or contextual evidence within the broader review framework. Methods: This review, registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF), followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. PubMed and Scopus were searched (final search: 5 August 2026), with PubMed Central used for full-text retrieval. Studies of rugby union players were eligible, and the direct-evidence studies were all match-based studies in male players from professional or elite amateur settings. Among 605 records identified, 11 studies were retained within the review framework: 4 as direct evidence and 7 as indirect or contextual evidence. Owing to differences in collision exposure definitions, biomarkers, post-match assessment times, and effect measures, evidence was synthesized narratively according to the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis guideline. Results: Four match-based studies (79 enrolled players in total) provided direct evidence for the review question. Three examined biochemical markers associated with muscle damage, specifically creatine kinase, myoglobin, and interstitial creatine kinase, but they differed in collision metrics, specimen types, and post-match sampling windows, which ranged from 30-45 min to 24 and 40 h. Across these studies, higher collision exposure was generally associated with greater post-match perturbation in these muscle-damage-related biochemical responses, although the clearest reported association in Jones et al. was limited to backs and the statistical detail available from Smart et al. was comparatively limited. One small study suggested that greater collision frequency was associated with poorer post-match sleep architecture; however, this finding should be interpreted as preliminary single-study evidence for a recovery-related outcome rather than an established physiological trend. Direct evidence regarding neuromuscular fatigue was insufficient. One indirect study reported increased post-match resting metabolic rate but did not examine its association with quantified collision exposure. Conclusions: Limited direct evidence links collision exposure to post-match recovery-related outcomes. The strongest signal concerns muscle-damage-associated biochemical markers, but this evidence is based on only three heterogeneous studies with limited cross-study comparability. Evidence concerning sleep architecture remains preliminary and is currently based on a single small study. These findings are correlational. Hence, future match-based studies should separate collision exposure from other workload measures and assess recovery-related outcomes across domains at standardized post-match time points.

title: Effects of different exercise and ischemic preconditioning strategies on muscle damage after low-load blood flow restriction exercise: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Originally developed to protect against ischemia-reperfusion injury, ischemic preconditioning (IPC) may also attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) after eccentric exercise. Blood flow restriction resistance training (BFR-RT) combines contractions under restricted perfusion with reperfusion, but whether IPC before BFR-RT protects against EIMD is unknown. This trial tested whether preconditioning before BFR-RT attenuates EIMD. Forty participants were randomized to no preconditioning (CON), low-load exercise without BFR (LL), low-load exercise with BFR at 50% arterial occlusion pressure (AOP) (LL-BFR), or IPC with three 5-min occlusions at 100% AOP and 5-min reperfusion. Fifteen minutes later, participants performed four sets of knee extensions to concentric failure at 30% one repetition maximum (1RM) and 50% AOP. Isometric, concentric, and eccentric peak torque (PT) were assessed through 72 h alongside creatine kinase, myoglobin, muscle soreness, and muscle thickness. No Group × Time interactions occurred for PT (all p ≥ .716). At 24 h, isometric, concentric, and eccentric PT were reduced by 6.69%, 8.10%, and 6.89%, respectively. Eccentric and isometric PT recovered by 48 h, whereas concentric PT remained reduced by 3.92% at 72 h. Markers showed small changes without group differences. None of the preconditioning strategies blunted EIMD. Despite mechanistic overlap between IPC and BFR-RT, the mild to moderate damage response may limit measurable preconditioning effects.

title: Effects of Intermittent Hypoxia in Sprint Interval Training on Performance and Physiological Responses: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Ribeiro, Felipe Alves, Germano Marcolino Putti, Júlia Causin Andreossi, Carlos Dellavechia de Carvalho, and Marcelo Papoti. Effects of intermittent hypoxia in sprint interval training on performance and physiological responses: a systematic review. High Alt Med Biol. 00:00-00, 2026.
OBJECTIVE: To synthesize the acute and chronic effects of sprint interval training (SIT) in hypoxia (SIH) on performance and physiological responses.
METHODS: This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Seven databases were searched from inception to August 14, 2025. Eligible studies compared hypoxic and normoxic conditions during acute or chronic SIT protocols comprising at least three repeated all-out efforts of 30 seconds interspersed by ∼4.5 minutes in healthy physically active or trained adults. Study selection, risk-of-bias assessment, and data extraction were conducted independently by two reviewers.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies were included, comprising 11 acute crossover studies and 7 chronic parallel-group studies. Seventeen studies used cycling and one tethered swimming. Acutely, peak power was generally preserved, whereas mean power and total work were more frequently impaired during severe or continuous hypoxia. Hypoxia often reduced peripheral oxygen saturation, oxygen uptake, peak oxygen uptake, muscle oxygen saturation, and oxyhemoglobin during exercise. Chronic SIT improved aerobic and performance outcomes, including oxygen uptake, time to exhaustion, time-trial performance, and critical power; however, SIH was not consistently superior to normoxic SIT.
CONCLUSIONS: SIH provides a substantial acute systemic and peripheral hypoxic stimulus, but its additional performance benefit remains inconsistent and appears to depend on hypoxic severity, hypoxic dose, recovery structure, and training status.

title: Dyslipidemia management in athletes: A comparative commentary on the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline and contemporary sports cardiology recommendations.
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death in athletes older than 35 years, and dyslipidemia is one of its principal modifiable drivers. The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol introduces several advances directly relevant to athletes, including restored LDL-C treatment targets, universal lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] measurement, the PREVENT-ASCVD risk equations, expanded options for selective coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring, and a more aggressive approach to lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). However, sports cardiology guidelines and consensus statements offer important caveats that must be reconciled with these general-population recommendations: existing risk calculators, including PREVENT, do not reliably estimate cardiovascular risk in athletes, and routine CAC scoring is not recommended in athletes at low calculated risk. This commentary compares and contrasts general-population dyslipidemia recommendations with athlete-specific guidance from contemporary sports cardiology consensus documents, highlights recent evidence on Lp(a), wearable-derived training load, and risk score performance across the physical activity spectrum, and proposes a five-step clinical framework, refined to reflect athlete-specific risk stratification, for dyslipidemia evaluation and management in this population.

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Inter-Effort Recovery Hypoxia On Repeated-Sprint Performance And Physiological Responses: A Randomized And Single-Blinded Crossover Trial.
abstract: We investigated the acute effects of local and/or systemic hypoxia on performance and psycho-physiological responses during repeated cycle sprints. Eleven physically active young adults (six men, five women) performed four sessions on separate days, each involving three sets of five 5-s all-out efforts on a cycle ergometer (25 seconds rest between efforts and 5 minutes rest between sets). Sessions were conducted under four conditions, combining blood flow restriction [BFR; 45% of arterial occlusion pressure (AOP)] or control (CON; 5% of AOP) applied bilaterally to the legs during sprints, with inter-effort recovery hypoxia [IEH; inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) = 13.5%] or normoxia (NOR; FiO2 = 20.9%). Power output decreased across sprints and heart rate increased over sets, with no differences between conditions (Δ = -9.18%). IEH resulted in lower peripheral oxygen saturation (Δ = -8.0%) but higher oxygen uptake (Δ = 6.7 mL·kg-1 min-1) and minute ventilation (Δ = 6.1 L·kg-1 min-1), compared to normoxic conditions. Blood lactate concentration increased (Δ = 6.5 mM) post-session similarly across all conditions. Vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation during sprints and inter-set recovery was comparable across conditions, although the mean tissue saturation index during inter-set recovery was lower in BFR + IEH versus CON + NOR conditions (Δ = -4.0%). Ratings of perceived exertion (Δ = 22.5%), limb discomfort (Δ = 34.2%), and breathing difficulty (Δ = 43.7%) increased throughout the sets, independently of conditions. Despite physiological and perceptual adjustments across sprint repetitions, neither BFR during sprints nor systemic hypoxia during recovery altered mechanical output in physically active individuals.

title: Evidence and Gaps in Rehabilitation Activation of Piezoelectric Nanomaterials for Musculoskeletal Repair.
abstract: Prescribed rehabilitation may activate piezoelectric nanomaterials, but exercise-associated repair, exercise-induced electrical generation, and an independent electrical benefit require different evidence. This targeted narrative review evaluates these propositions in cartilage, bone, tendon and enthesis, and skeletal muscle. Primary studies were classified by prescribed exercise, spontaneous physiological loading, external ultrasound, or bench activation, and by whether they measured electrical exposure, structural repair, biomechanics, or behavior. Rabbit cartilage and rat tendon-to-bone studies provide exercise-associated proof of concept; they do not establish a reproducible in vivo electrical dose or durable functional recovery. Ultrasound studies support electromechanical plausibility under a different trigger, while bone and muscle evidence has limited direct rehabilitation relevance. Fiber alignment, particle dispersion, and scaffold geometry influence local deformation and charge generation, but also change mechanics and cell interactions. Calcium-dependent endogenous TGF-β signaling has been reported in specific PLLA systems; general ion-channel and integrin-FAK/YAP/TAZ pathways cannot be assigned to every piezoelectric construct. We propose an assessment pathway linking activity, implant strain, wet-state electrical exposure, biological response, and independently measured function. This pathway identifies missing measurements and controls rather than providing a calibrated dose-conversion rule. Prospective validation, matched inactive scaffolds, fatigue and release measurements, and functional outcomes are needed before clinical rehabilitation dosing can be justified.

title: Survey Findings From Orthopaedic Surgeons in Asia-Pacific: Attitudes and Practice Patterns in Pediatric Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate current anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction rehabilitation recommendations among Asia-Pacific orthopaedic surgeons and compare them with previously published North American data.
METHODS: An online survey was conducted between January 2024 and June 2025, distributed to all orthopaedic surgeons within Pediatric Research in Sports Medicine Asia-Pacific in 2024, capturing clinical practice patterns at 3 key milestones: initiation of jogging, progression to modified sports activity, and unrestricted return to sport. Only orthopaedic surgeons within Pediatric Research in Sports Medicine Asia-Pacific who had provided informed consent to participate were included. The results were compared with a previously published survey of North American surgeons.
RESULTS: The survey was sent to 127 surgeons, and 54 (43%) responded. Agreement was greatest for jogging-80% recommending initiation at 3 to 4 months postoperatively. Consensus declined for later phases: modified sports activity between 4 and 8 months, whereas return to sport spanned from 6 to 12 months. Compared with Pediatric Research in Sports Medicine North America, where 92% allowed jogging at 3 to 4 months and return to sport often advised at 6 to 9 months, Asia-Pacific surgeons showed a delayed approach. Asia-Pacific respondents considered quadriceps and hamstring strength essential for progression, although modalities varied-manual muscle testing (60%) predominated over isokinetic (28%) or isometric (12%) methods. Functional testing was employed by 68% prior to modified sports activity, with variability in test type and criteria. Compared with North American peers, Asia-Pacific surgeons used more objective strength and functional assessments, with limited use of patient-reported outcomes (20%). At the time of return to sport, 73% recommended injury-prevention programs and 50% endorsed functional bracing, rates comparable to North America.
CONCLUSIONS: Acknowledging the temporal differences between both surveys and the evolution of rehabilitation practices during this period, the present study suggests a tendency toward conservative rehabilitation timelines in the Asia-Pacific region, with respect to return to jogging, return to modified sporting activity, and unrestricted return to sport. Strength and functional assessments are valued highly across both surveys, although differences exist in specific testing modalities employed and criteria used to guide progression.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This survey-based comparison provides insight into regional variation and temporal trends in surgeon-reported anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction rehabilitation practices. The findings may assist clinicians and researchers in contextualizing contemporary rehabilitation recommendations and highlight areas of variability that warrant further standardization.

title: Increases in Agility and Quantitative Movement Quality Following a Coach-Led, Basketball-Specific Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Programme in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coach-led, basketball-specific neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up programs have been shown to reduce injury risk. However, changes in agility and movement quality following such NMT in high school basketball players are not well characterized.
METHODS: In this pre-experimental study, high school basketball players (42 males, 31 females, 16 ± 1.4 years) performed a 10-minute, coach-led, basketball-specific NMT warm-up programme before practices and games (10-14 weeks). Changes in the Lane Agility Test (LAT) and single-leg squat (SLS) kinematics, encompassing trunk, pelvis, hip, and lower extremity kinematics and a composite score (SLS Score), from pre-to post-intervention were assessed. Relationships between pre-intervention scores, sex, the number of NMT sessions completed, and outcomes were assessed with linear regressions.
RESULTS: LAT completion times decreased following the NMT intervention, with larger changes associated with slower pre-intervention scores and more completed NMT sessions. SLS Scores were higher after the NMT intervention, potentially attributable to better pelvic and hip kinematics.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm preliminary and exploratory study, favourable changes in agility and SLS kinematics following a coach-led, basketball-specific NMT programme were observed, with preliminary evidence of a dose-response relationship for agility. However, this study was non-randomized and lacked a control group. Therefore, these results should not be interpreted to suggest a causal relationship between the NMT performed and the changes in outcomes. In addition to NMT's role in injury prevention, coaches and players should be cognizant about performance and movement quality changes potentially associated with this accessible version of NMT.

title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.
