title: Body recomposition in adults: mechanisms, modulators, and practical algorithms for simultaneous skeletal muscle mass gain and fat mass loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Body recomposition is the concurrent increase in fat-free mass (FFM) or skeletal muscle mass and decrease in fat mass (FM) within the same intervention period. Although hypertrophy is commonly pursued in energy surplus and FM loss in energy deficit, controlled trials indicate that recomposition can occur when progressive resistance training (PRT), adequate protein intake, and an appropriate energy prescription are combined.
METHODS: We conducted a structured narrative review of randomised trials, meta-analyses, and selected mechanistic studies in adults, with emphasis on FFM, FM, strength, and performance outcomes. Device heterogeneity was considered when interpreting evidence, with greatest weight placed on four-compartment and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) outcomes.
RESULTS: PRT combined with higher protein intake, typically ~1.6-2.4 g/kg/day and higher relative intakes during energy restriction or leanness, is the most consistent strategy for recomposition. Effects are largest in untrained individuals and those with higher adiposity, smaller in trained or lean athletes, and still feasible in older adults when anabolic resistance is addressed with supervised PRT and sufficient protein. Moderate deficits, carbohydrate allocation around key sessions, sleep, and recovery support FFM retention or accretion while facilitating FM loss. Practical applications: Programmes should pair progressive overload with protein-centred diets, modest energy deficits, and periodic monitoring of body composition and performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Body recomposition is feasible but context-dependent; expected changes are generally modest in trained or lean populations and require individualised adjustment.

title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

title: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition and quadriceps activation failure after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: Early assessment and rehabilitation beyond strength.
abstract: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) is common in the early postoperative period after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and can persist throughout rehabilitation. However, clinically assessing AMI is challenging, typically requiring muscle stimulation-based testing with dynamometry and/or electromyography (EMG) to estimate the precise degree of quadriceps activation failure. However, a reliable clinical examination can identify and grade the overt contraction impairment, extension loss and hamstring contracture often associated with laboratory assayed AMI. A recent report found 49% of patients at 3 weeks and 24% at 6 weeks after ACLR present with at least one clinically detectable sign of likely AMI. Preoperative clinical AMI, greater immediate postoperative pain and absence of preoperative physiotherapy were associated with higher prevalence of clinical AMI at 3 weeks, highlighting the vital nature of early physiotherapy and pain management. As the patient progresses, since AMI refers to the neural inhibition of the muscle secondary to joint injury, strength gains can actually coexist with persistent activation deficits. Thus, traditional strengthening programs may not be achieving optimal efficiency when attempting to restore strength after joint injury. Rehabilitation that integrates activation exercises, symptom management and progressive strengthening, with neuromuscular electrical stimulation and/or biofeedback may reduce AMI and enhance recovery. At return to sport, strength recovery should not be interpreted as proof of activation recovery and specialised muscle activation testing should be considered selectively when clinical testing is inconclusive. Future studies should determine whether identifying and treating activation deficits improves functional recovery and informs safer return-to-sport decisions.

title: Global Perspective in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Soccer Players: Current Concepts for the 2026 World Cup.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in soccer players represent a major challenge in modern sports medicine, particularly among elite athletes. Despite significant advances in surgical techniques, graft biology, and rehabilitation protocols graft failure rates, reinjury, and suboptimal return-to-sport outcomes remain clinically relevant concerns. Contemporary approaches emphasize a multifactorial strategy encompassing injury prevention, individualized graft selection, restoration of rotational and multiplanar stability, meniscal preservation, and criteria-based return-to-sport progression. Data from global registries and patient groups show that graft failure rates approach 10% for all types of grafts. This highlights the importance of a more holistic surgical approach that addresses the entire knee rather than focusing solely on replacing individual ligaments. There is growing evidence that adding lateral extra-articular procedures reduces failure rates, especially in high-risk athletes such as soccer players where cutting and pivoting are common. It is also crucial to recognize and treat concomitant injuries including meniscal tears, posterior meniscal root injuries, and medial instability to improve long-term outcomes. It is important to provide a comprehensive overview of anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in soccer players, integrating insights from an international symposium held in 2026 with the latest evidence available. Key areas covered include injury prevention strategies, biomechanics of injuries, graft selection, restoration of rotational stability, meniscal function preservation, rehabilitation approaches, and future directions for personalized medicine.

title: Performance-Centred Weight Management: A Harm-Reduction Framework for Emerging Body Mass Interventions in Sport.
abstract: Highly effective incretin-based therapies are increasingly extending beyond obesity treatment into fitness, body image, and sporting environments, raising new questions regarding athletes' health, informed decision-making, performance enhancement, and off-label use. Direct extrapolation of evidence from obesity medicine to athletes is inappropriate because body mass management in sport must preserve training adaptation and physiological readiness for competition. This Perspective proposes Performance-Centred Weight Management (PCWM), a health-oriented conceptual framework intended to guide the evaluation of traditional weight-cutting practices, nutritional interventions, structured exercise programmes, incretin-based therapies, and future body mass interventions in sport. PCWM integrates five interdependent domains: muscle quality and function, energy availability, recovery and training adaptation, sport-specific performance capacity, and long-term athlete health and wellbeing, within a model of longitudinal monitoring aligned with training periodisation. PCWM distinguishes evaluation from endorsement. Rather than considering body mass reduction as the primary endpoint, the framework identifies physiological readiness for competition, athlete health, and informed decision-making as the principal outcomes of successful body mass management. By integrating performance-oriented assessment with medical supervision and harm-minimisation principles, PCWM offers a conceptual basis for evaluating emerging pharmacological body mass interventions. However, the framework has not yet undergone empirical validation, and its feasibility, clinical utility, and applicability across sporting disciplines require further investigation. Future research should examine off-label use, access pathways, risk perception, sport-specific physiological outcomes, and potential interactions between pharmacological appetite suppression, low energy availability, and training adaptation.

title: Clinical Assessments to Inform Return to Play Prognosis Following Acute Hamstring Injury: An Evidence-Informed Guide for Clinicians.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rehabilitation clinicians aim to provide a return to play (RTP) prognosis following acute hamstring injury based on various clinical assessments, including subjective interview questions and physical examinations. CLINICAL QUESTION: What subjective interview questions and physical examinations should be prioritised during an initial clinical assessment following acute hamstring injury to inform RTP? KEY RESULTS: There are key subjective interview questions and physical examination findings to inform RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury. Prolonged RTP time has been associated with athletes who: 1) recall higher pain ratings at the time of injury; 2) report pain with palpation closer to the ischial tuberosity; 3) have greater cranio-caudal length of palpable pain; 4) present with between-leg deficits of greater magnitude in maximal hip flexion active knee extension range of motion and isometric knee flexion strength in outer-range (supine with 90° hip/knee flexion) and/or mid-range (prone with 0° hip and ~15° knee flexion); and 4) experience pain during outer-range hamstring contraction. CLINICAL APPLICATION: This evidence-informed clinical commentary may help clinicians prioritise subjective interview questions and physical examinations to inform their RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury.

title: Arthrogenic Muscle Inhibition and Quadriceps Dysfunction After Primary and Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) reliably relieves pain in end-stage knee osteoarthritis, but quadriceps dysfunction may continue to limit walking, stair climbing, balance, and confidence. This narrative review examines arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) and quadriceps dysfunction after primary and revision TKA. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception through August 2026 using terms related to AMI, quadriceps activation, TKA, and rehabilitation. Relevant studies were selected for narrative synthesis, prioritizing direct TKA evidence and identifying evidence from other knee populations as indirect. AMI is impaired voluntary activation associated with altered joint afferent input and neural inhibition, whereas atrophy reflects loss of muscle tissue. Both can coexist and contribute to weakness. Surgical trauma, pain, effusion, inflammation, altered proprioception, and immobilization may impair early motor-unit recruitment. Preoperative weakness, inactivity, obesity, comorbidity, and revision surgery may further reduce physiological reserve. Muscle-preserving exposure may improve selected early outcomes, but must not compromise safe exposure or component positioning. Revision procedures add tissue injury, extensor-mechanism risk, systemic illness, and rehabilitation restrictions; direct voluntary-activation evidence after revision TKA remains limited. Assessment should combine strength and functional testing with measures of voluntary activation and muscle morphology when feasible. Management includes pain and swelling control, safe early activation, progressive strengthening, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, selected blood-flow-restriction training, motor-control rehabilitation, and targeted prehabilitation. Nutritional and laboratory assessment can identify modifiable risks but does not diagnose AMI. A practical perioperative framework is proposed to support identification and management of quadriceps dysfunction after primary and revision TKA.

title: The knee replacement that never happened: a case of recovery following structured neuromuscular rehabilitation.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and reduced mobility, often leading patients to consider total knee replacement (TKR). Exercise is recommended as part of treatment; however, there is little guidance on the optimal type or duration of rehabilitation before surgery. As a result, some patients may be listed for TKR before receiving a structured trial of nonoperative care. We report the case of a 78-year-old woman with symptomatic knee OA placed on a National Health Service waiting list for TKR. While awaiting surgery, she undertook the Awareness, Resistance, Individualized, Stability, and Essential OrthoPrehab programme, a structured neuromuscular rehabilitation programme focusing on joint awareness, movement control, proprioception, and strengthening. After 3 months, she experienced improvements in pain, function, and confidence, reduced reliance on analgesics, and withdrew from the surgical waiting list. This case highlights the potential of structured rehabilitation to help some patients avoid surgery.

title: Imaging and diagnosis of overuse shoulder injuries in overhead athletes.
abstract: Shoulder overuse injuries are highly prevalent among athletes participating in overhead sports such as baseball, tennis, swimming, and volleyball, where repetitive high-velocity loading imposes unique biomechanical demands on the glenohumeral complex. These injuries span a broad spectrum, including rotator cuff tears, subacromial/subdeltoid impingement, superior labrum anterior-to-posterior (SLAP) lesions, long head of the biceps tendinopathy, glenohumeral instability, internal impingement, glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD), and Little League shoulder. Accurate diagnosis requires an understanding of sport-specific biomechanics, particularly the extreme forces generated during the late cocking and early acceleration phases of throwing, which produce characteristic injury patterns such as posterosuperior partial articular-sided rotator cuff tears and type II SLAP lesions via the peel-back mechanism. Imaging plays a central role in diagnosis and management. Radiographs remain the initial study for evaluating osseous anatomy and acromial morphology. MRI is the principal modality for soft-tissue assessment, while MR arthrography offers superior sensitivity for intra-articular pathology, including labral and partial articular-sided rotator cuff tears. Musculoskeletal ultrasound provides dynamic, cost-effective evaluation of tendons and bursae, and 3D CT or zero-time echo (ZTE) MRI is essential for quantifying glenoid bone loss in the setting of instability. Because many imaging findings are present in asymptomatic athletes, careful clinical correlation is essential. This review summarizes the imaging features, diagnostic pearls, and limitations of current modalities for shoulder overuse injuries in overhead athletes.

title: Ultrasound-guided needling release combined with platelet-rich plasma injection for refractory heel pain: A case report.
abstract:
RATIONALE: Refractory heel pain is a clinically challenging condition of multifactorial origin, often complicating both diagnosis and treatment. No standard therapy exists for refractory heel pain, and clinical experience is limited. We report the efficacy of ultrasound-guided needling release of calcific deposits combined with autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection and systematic rehabilitation in a patient with refractory heel pain.
PATIENT CONCERNS: A 57-year-old self-employed female patient presented with a 3-year history of recurrent redness, swelling, and pain in the right heel, with symptoms worsening after activity. In the month prior to admission, pain had progressively worsened, limiting her ability to stand, walk, and perform daily activities.
DIAGNOSES: Refractory right heel pain (chronic calcifying Achilles tendinitis, Achilles tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis with bone spur formation).
INTERVENTIONS: The procedure involved ultrasound-guided fenestration and disruption of calcifications at the Achilles tendon insertion, followed by intralesional PRP injection and a 6-month staged rehabilitation program.
OUTCOMES: At 1 week postoperatively, Visual Analog Scale (VAS) decreased to 3, and the patient could walk independently. At 1 month, VAS was 2, and she returned to work and daily activities. At 3 months, VAS was 1, American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society score improved to 90, and pain was largely resolved. The favorable outcome persisted at 6-month follow-up.
LESSONS: The combination of ultrasound-guided precise lesion management, PRP-based biological repair, and systematic rehabilitation offers a minimally invasive, safe, and effective strategy for refractory heel pain, serving as a valuable clinical reference for similar cases.

title: Arthroscopic Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation Using Specialized Instrumentation for Exposure, Preparation, and Delivery.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI) has been recognized as a leading option for treating large articular cartilage defects in the knee1,4. MACI (Vericel) is the current generation of ACI available for use in the United States and consists of autologous cultured chondrocytes seeded onto a resorbable type-I/III porcine collagen membrane4. For years, MACI implantation has required an arthrotomy in order to implant the membrane; however, in August 2024, the U.S. Food & Drug Administration (FDA) approved a supplemental Biologics License Application expanding the MACI label to include arthroscopic delivery to repair cartilage defects of the knee up to 4 cm2 in size. Arthroscopic delivery of the MACI implant represents a new approach that is less invasive. The present video article provides a step-by-step process for delivering the MACI membrane via an arthroscopic approach with use of specially designed MACI Arthro instruments (Vericel). Following proper preoperative planning, positioning, and surgical exposure, the arthroscopic technique involves defect preparation with curets and arthroscopic cutters, creation of a dry environment, and secure delivery of the cell-seeded membrane with use of a dedicated cannula and delivery system.
DESCRIPTION: The arthroscopic technique begins with preoperative planning, including portal selection to achieve a perpendicular approach to the lesion, which may be more straightforward for medial condylar defects and more challenging for lateral condylar lesions. After positioning and surgical exposure, a specialized arthroscopic instrument set, including cannulas, cutters, curets, and a delivery device, is utilized to measure and prepare the lesion. A dry arthroscopic field is established for membrane delivery, preferably without the use of a tourniquet. The chondrocyte-seeded membrane is trimmed to the exact size of the defect and is delivered into the defect with use of a dedicated delivery system. The graft is positioned and is secured with use of fibrin glue in the dry joint environment in order to ensure stability and integration. Rehabilitation follows the standard MACI protocol, despite the less-invasive arthroscopic approach, and has 4 stages based on the status of the graft (0 to 6 weeks, protection and motion; 6 to 12 weeks, transition and proliferation; 12 to 26 weeks, remodeling; >26 weeks, maturation). To optimize graft maturation, the recommended postoperative regimen is continuous passive motion for 3 weeks, followed by the use of a brace locked in extension while walking for 6 weeks, and then progressive physical therapy.
ALTERNATIVES: An alternative to the presently described procedure is the use of an open MACI technique.
RATIONALE: Arthroscopic MACI is less invasive than the use of an open MACI technique.
EXPECTED OUTCOMES: In a series of studies, research teams from the University of Western Australia evaluated arthroscopic delivery of the MACI membrane, introducing the membrane into the knee via a large-bore, valveless arthroscopic cannula. In a 12-month study, early outcomes of the technique were encouraging among the first 10 prospectively assessed patients. Patients reported less pain and better symptom scores per the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), as compared with previously reported open MACI outcomes4. In an additional 24-month study, outcomes in 20 patients further supported the feasibility and safety of the arthroscopic technique. Significant improvements were noted across all KOOS subscales postoperatively, although without a control group the true treatment effect could not be isolated. MRI findings also demonstrated progressive morphologic graft repair over 24 months, with 90% of patients showing good-to-excellent graft infill and 70% achieving a good-to-excellent overall MRI composite score at 24 months. These results indicate that the technique is safe and rfeasible, with improved clinical and radiographic outcomes over the 2-year follow-up period1. In a third study of the first 31 patients who underwent arthroscopic MACI, 93% reported being satisfied with their pain level postoperatively. Additionally, 90% reported being satisfied with improvements in their ability to undertake daily activities, and 80% had improvements in participating in sports. Graft infill significantly improved over time, with 90% of patients demonstrating good-to-excellent tissue infill at 5 years postoperatively. There were 2 graft failures (6%) at 5 years postoperatively. The authors concluded that arthroscopic MACI demonstrated strong clinical and radiographic outcomes with high patient satisfaction up to 5 years postoperatively2. A retrospective study comparing the arthroscopic technique to a mini-open approach demonstrated better active knee range of motion and strength and fewer postoperative complications with use of the arthroscopic approach3.
IMPORTANT TIPS: Ensure that the portal allows for a perpendicular approach to the defect.Place the cutting guide toward the edge of the membrane; this allows for additional membrane harvest if needed, as well as easy removal of the membrane once it has been cut.The membrane should be the same size as or slightly smaller (rather than slightly larger) than the articular cartilage defect; the MACI should cover the prepared defect without overhanging margins.
ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS: DVT = deep venous thrombosisMRI = magnetic resonance imaging.

title: Should Nerve Transfer Surgery be the Standard of Care for Cervical Spinal Cord Injury?
abstract: Nerve transfer surgery is a promising intervention to improve upper limb function following cervical spinal cord injury, but there are knowledge gaps about optimal candidates, surgical timing, rehabilitation, and outcomes. The purpose of this review is to provide a critical analysis of the literature for nerve transfer surgery in this population, while also emphasizing the difficulty in generating high-quality evidence in this field. We establish that the outcomes from nerve transfer are on aggregate positive, but the individual response can be variable. We also discuss several aspects that have not been previously considered: (1) peri-operative challenges such as the optimal timing of the intervention in a complicated clinical milieu; (2) the potential benefits of combining nerve and tendon transfer in the same limb; (3) how nerve transfer surgery may be affected by and how it can potentially improve spasticity. Finally, we will introduce newly characterized central and peripheral nerve system barriers to nerve transfer rehabilitation, which necessitate novel combinatorial approaches to optimize patient outcomes.

title: The Unique Features of Pediatric Sports Injuries: Shoulder Instability-Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Dislocations.
abstract: Traumatic anterior shoulder dislocations are common in youth athletes and occur more frequently in males and older adolescents. Dislocations typically result from direct trauma to the arm while in extension, abduction, and external rotation. Other risk factors include increased skeletal maturity and joint laxity. Inspection is a key component of the physical examination in the acute postdislocation setting, whereas provocative instability tests are useful for eliciting a history of dislocation. A standard two-view radiographic protocol is recommended for any patient with a first-time dislocation, and advanced imaging facilitates more reliable identification of concomitant bony and soft-tissue injuries such as Hill-Sachs and Bankart lesions. Management is guided by age, structural abnormalities, likelihood of recurrence, and other patient-specific factors. Nonsurgical treatment features brief immobilization followed by progressive rehabilitation, whereas surgical treatment focuses on surgically repairing shoulder stabilizers. Despite high return-to-sport rates in the pediatric and adolescent population, the risk of recurrent dislocations is also high.

title: The Unique Features of Pediatric Sports Injuries: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Pediatric and Adolescent Patients.
abstract: Pediatric anterior cruciate ligament injuries represent a substantial portion of skeletally immature knee injuries. Assessment and management of these injuries are multifactorial, and consideration of remaining growth helps inform appropriate management. Although many patients can return to their baseline level of activity after treatment, there is a considerable risk of reinjury in this patient population. Concomitant procedures such as lateral extra-articular tenodesis and attention to postoperative physical therapy may help reduce the risk of complications.

title: Return to sports after pediatric brain tumors: Time to move beyond survival.
abstract: Brain tumors are the second most common malignancy in children and adolescents and the leading cause of cancer-related death in this population. While survival rates have improved, survivors are at risk of neurocognitive, motor, and psychosocial sequelae due to both tumor location and treatments used. Participation in sport is increasingly recognized as beneficial for functional recovery, cardiorespiratory fitness, and overall well-being in children and adolescents treated for brain tumors. However, return to play (RTP) may pose some challenges, particularly in the presence of neurosurgical devices, cranial radiotherapy, or residual neurological deficits. This narrative clinical review summarizes current evidence on the risks of sport-related injuries in pediatric brain tumor patients and survivors, highlighting factors influencing vulnerability, including treatment history and specific sport characteristics. We propose a risk-based framework for RTP evaluation emphasizing individualized coordinated assessment by pediatric oncologists, neurosurgeons, and sports medicine specialists. Protective strategies are discussed, although evidence for concussion prevention remains limited. A safe RTP should be enhanced by the here-proposed structured evaluation, balancing safety with the physical, cognitive, and psychosocial benefits of active participation. This framework aims to support clinicians and families in facilitating safe and effective reintegration of pediatric brain tumor survivors into both recreational and competitive sports.

title: Bucket-Handle Meniscus Tears.
abstract: Bucket-handle meniscus tears represent a distinct and surgically significant pattern of meniscal injury, most commonly occurring in young, active patients and frequently associated with anterior cruciate ligament injury. The displaced central fragment produces a mechanical block to terminal knee extension, requiring prompt recognition and surgical intervention. Meniscal preservation through repair is the preferred approach when tissue quality and vascularity permit. It is important to review the diagnosis, surgical indications, repair techniques, and postoperative rehabilitation of bucket-handle meniscus tears, with a focus on evidence-based decision making for single-stage versus two-stage surgery, inside-out versus all-inside repair, adjunct techniques such as medial collateral ligament pie crusting and biologic augmentation, and criteria-based return to sport.

title: Orthobiologics 2026: State of the Art.
abstract: Orthobiologics are biologic products intended to promote healing and manage a range of musculoskeletal conditions. The field has evolved from a loosely defined collection of regenerative products into one that increasingly demands product-specific biology, indication-specific evidence, and disciplined postmarket surveillance. The strongest current clinical support remains for platelet-rich plasma for selected knee osteoarthritis and tendinopathy indications, whereas platelet-poor plasma may represent a distinct muscle-healing strategy. Cell-based therapies such as concentrated bone marrow aspirate and adipose-derived products remain biologically appealing but clinically heterogeneous, with outcomes influenced by harvest technique, processing method, route of administration, host phenotype, and disease severity. Perinatal tissue products, exosomes, and gene therapy occupy different positions on the translational spectrum: amniotic or placental products have the most mature clinical programs among emerging orthobiologic therapies, exosomes remain predominantly preclinical and highly regulated, and intra-articular gene transfer has now entered human trials with sustained transgene expression. A recurring theme across all presentations was that orthobiologics should no longer be studied as black-box interventions. Instead, progress will depend on linking clinical outcomes to rigorous product characterization, biomarker analysis, and scalable registry infrastructure. The Biologics Association Registry and Biorepository and the linked American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Orthobiologics Registry represent an important attempt to generate real-world evidence while simultaneously measuring the biologic content of what is injected. It is important to summarize the state of the art across blood-derived products, cell-based therapies, advanced acellular therapeutics, and registry science and outline the priorities that should guide orthopaedic practice and research over the next cycle of orthobiologic development.

title: Adhesive and Antibacterial Bio-Based Hydrogel for Human Voice Recognition and Osteoarthritis Recovery Monitoring.
abstract: Conductive hydrogels derived from natural polysaccharides hold great promise for next generation wearable electronics owing to their intrinsic biocompatibility, adhesiveness, and tunable mechanical properties. However, realizing amylum-based hydrogels with simultaneously high stretchability, sensitivity, strong adhesion and antibacterial performance remains a significant challenge. Herein, a multifunctional ionic hydrogel, marked as PAPC4 hydrogel, composed of polyacrylamide (PAAm), amylum and phenol-modified chitosan is developed via a one-pot synthesis strategy. The hydrogel exhibits exceptional stretchability (up to 1605%), short response time (16.1 ms), high optical transparency (96%), strong adhesion (43.2 kPa on PVC) and pronounced antibacterial activity. Cytotoxicity assays, live/dead staining, and subcutaneous implantation supported its biocompatibility under the tested conditions, while bacterial assays demonstrated activity against Escherichia coli. As a strain sensor, PAPC4 detected joint movements and throat vibrations during speech. It also recorded differences in knee movement among control, osteoarthritis, and treated osteoarthritis groups in rats. These results support the use of this chitosan-starch composite hydrogel in wearable motion sensing and rehabilitation monitoring.

title: Arthroscopic technique for anterior cruciate ligament repair augmented with an internal brace: Current technique.
abstract: Primary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) repair serves as a joint-preserving surgical option for carefully selected acute proximal ACL tears (Sherman Type I and II) presenting within 4 weeks of injury. The proximal ACL stump is secured using high-strength FiberWire sutures, which are passed through the adjustable loop of a cortical button incorporating a FiberTape suture that acts as an internal brace. The distal ends of the repair sutures and internal brace tape are subsequently fixed to the proximal anteromedial tibial cortex using an externally attachable button system. Compared with conventional ACL reconstruction, primary repair aims to preserve the native ACL stump and its proprioceptive mechanoreceptors, which may theoretically maintain dynamic stability and physiological knee kinematics while avoiding donor-site morbidity. The internal brace acts as a secondary mechanical stabilizer during the early healing phase, sharing loads to prevent gap formation and protect the biological repair during early motion. This technical note describes patient selection criteria, portal placement, precise construct assembly, differential knee-flexion tensioning, and a criteria-based postoperative rehabilitation protocol.

title: The Ankle's Roll in Landing: Insights Into ACL Injury Biomechanics.
abstract: Noncontact ACL injuries typically occur within the first 40 milliseconds after ground contact, before voluntary neuromuscular responses can alter joint loading. This study quantified whether early ankle and foot mechanics during single-leg landing are associated with knee biomechanics within an ACL injury-relevant timeframe. Forty-one recreationally active adults performed a horizontal-to-vertical single-leg hop, while kinematics and ground reaction forces were recorded. Gradient-boosted decision tree models with participant-wise leave-one-subject-out cross-validation and nested feature selection were used to predict knee outcomes from ankle mechanics and participant descriptors. Knee-flexion displacement demonstrated the strongest predictive performance (R2 = .430), with greater ankle dorsiflexion at initial contact associated with reduced knee-flexion displacement. Across its interquartile range, initial-contact dorsiflexion was associated with a 4.36° reduction in predicted knee-flexion displacement. Knee-extensor yield impulse demonstrated the next-highest R2 (.334), with greater magnitude early plantarflexor yield impulse associated with greater knee-extensor yield impulse (0.0160 N·m·s·kg-1 across its interquartile range). Frontal-plane knee outcomes and peak vertical ground reaction force were poorly predicted. These findings identify initial-contact ankle-dorsiflexion and early plantarflexor yield impulse as distal variables associated with selected sagittal-plane knee outcomes during early landing.

title: FoRist: Three-DoF Soft Wearable Robot for Forearm and Wrist Assistance.
abstract: The growing population of elderly individuals affected by musculoskeletal and neurological diseases experiences multijoint functional impairment, and individuals with compromised forearm and wrist function can lose independence and quality of life. However, most wearable robotic devices provide assistance for a single degree of freedom (DoF) and restrict other joint movements because decoupling multijoint kinematics remains challenging. This article introduces FoRist, a lightweight three-DoF soft wearable robot designed for forearm and wrist assistance. FoRist assists wrist ulnar/radial deviation, wrist extension/flexion, and forearm pronation/supination through a spring blade-based active-passive hybrid actuation mechanism using three motors. It integrates compact rail structures, soft tension transfer mechanisms, and a flexible twisted string actuation mechanism to assist forearm-wrist motion while preserving freedom of movement in the neighboring hand and elbow joints. The local wearable structure at the wristband rail-slider engagement has a maximum thickness of 16 mm. Its personalized usability features, including bioanatomical analysis-driven customization and user-friendly donning/doffing, support application to individuals with forearm and wrist impairments. User tests with stroke survivors showed that wearing FoRist increased the achievable range of motion and output torque across the forearm and wrist movements compared with unassisted movement. In a two-participant test of a simulated food-preparation sequence involving opening a jar, scooping jam, and spreading jam on bread, FoRist assistance increased task-relevant wrist motion and was associated with lower maximum shoulder abduction. These preliminary results support FoRist's feasibility and usability in short-term laboratory use. With its compact three-DoF architecture, low distal mass, and personalized fit, FoRist offers a promising avenue for extending rehabilitation training beyond clinical settings and has the potential to enhance independence and functional performance in activities of daily living.

title: Hydration-Driven Self-Strengthening Silk Fibroin Ionic Elastomer for Electro-Immunomodulatory Achilles Tendon Repair.
abstract: Achilles tendon repair remains limited by fibrotic healing and implants' inability to coordinate mechanical support, ionic signaling, electrical cues, and immune remodeling in wet load-bearing environments. We report a bioinspired self-strengthening silk fibroin ionic elastomer (SFIE) as an electro-immunomodulatory artificial Achilles tendon. Lithium chloride is integrated into regenerated silk fibroin to create a hydration-responsive protein-ion network. Upon water uptake, LiCl-associated hydration may facilitate chain mobility and the reorganization of hydrophobic silk domains into β-sheet nanocrystals, enhancing tensile strength and modulus while preserving extensibility, fatigue resistance, and ionic conductivity. SFIE sustains Li+ release within a bioactive window that supports bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) viability and tenogenic activity. Mechanistically, SFIE-derived Li+ is associated with altered BMSC paracrine signaling, including reduced arachidonic acid secretion, which may modulate macrophage inflammatory responses. These effects are associated with changes in cPLA2/DUSP3/p38-related signaling. With electrical stimulation, SFIE increases intracellular Ca2 + levels and is associated with changes in CaM/CREB/NR4A1/LIF-related signaling and reduced CXCL10 secretion, potentially contributing to altered macrophage recruitment. In a rat Achilles tendon defect model, SFIE plus electrical stimulation improves gait recovery, tendon continuity, collagen alignment, tendon-marker expression, and local immune remodeling. This work establishes a self-strengthening ionic protein elastomer for functional tendon repair.

title: Understanding the Complexity of Athlete Sleep: A Systems Approach to Modelling the Athlete Sleep Environment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athlete sleep can be disrupted by sport- and non-sport-related factors. However, the interactions of these sleep-related factors are not well understood. Systems science approaches, such as causal loop diagramming (CLD), provide an opportunity to map these interactions. This project aimed to (1) develop a CLD of the athlete sleep system describing the interacting variables, (2) identify feedback loops and potential leverage points to optimise athlete sleep, and (3) demonstrate the applicability of a CLD to guide the development of a sleep monitoring framework.
METHODS: A systems-based model of athlete sleep was developed using CLD, informed by existing literature and refined through a consensus process involving ten subject matter experts (nine from Australia, one from the USA). The model was then interrogated using network analysis to identify key variables based on their position and connectivity within the system. These findings informed the development of a generic sleep monitoring framework.
RESULTS: The CLD comprised 48 variables and 120 relationships across four domains: travel demands, behavioural and lifestyle factors, athlete condition and readiness, and resourcing and scheduling constraints. Overall, 12 key variables were identified, with hours of travel, number of time zones crossed, dose of caffeine, and amount of resources or expenditure available being the most connected upstream variables. Level of pre-sleep arousal, sleep opportunity, travel fatigue, and level of performance received the greatest number of incoming relationships, representing points at which multiple pathways converge. Physical condition, level of performance, quality of diet, and importance of competition most frequently linked different quadrants of the system. These variables informed a three-tier monitoring framework capturing upstream determinants and downstream consequences of sleep.
CONCLUSIONS: According to the CLD, sleep health in athletes extends beyond an individual behaviour issue and is influenced by the structure and functioning of sport systems. Interactions among travel demands, physical readiness, behavioural and lifestyle factors, and organisational constraints sustain athlete sleep health over time. Consequently, meaningful improvements in sleep health are likely to arise from both system-level interventions and individual behaviour change strategies.

title: Hybrid multimodal exercise training promotes enhanced recovery after surgery and improves musculoskeletal strength in patients with osteosarcopenic obesity: A clinical study protocol.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Osteosarcopenic obesity (OSO) is a progressive, systemic condition characterized by declines in skeletal muscle mass, strength, and function, accompanied by bone loss and adipose tissue accumulation, leading to adverse health outcomes including frailty, poor quality of life, high fracture risk, poor postoperative recovery, and mortality. It is more common in older adults, with physical inactivity and malnutrition being the main etiological factors, especially lack of exercise. Regular physical activity combined with appropriate dietary intervention is necessary to achieve optimal therapeutic effects for OSO. However, conventional exercise may be difficult for older adults with OSO who often present with frailty, and little is known about the role of exercise in promoting enhanced recovery after surgery and improving musculoskeletal strength in OSO patients. Hybrid multimodal exercise training, which involves targeted training based on an individual's physical and health status, may benefit bone, muscle, and quality of life. This clinical study investigates the feasibility and effectiveness of hybrid multimodal exercise training in promoting enhanced recovery after surgery and improving musculoskeletal strength in patients with osteosarcopenic obesity.
METHODS AND DESIGN: One hundred and twenty older adults diagnosed with OSO will be assigned to two groups: a hybrid multimodal exercise training group and a usual care group. Assessments will be conducted in the hospital, including baseline and post-intervention evaluations of health and function (body composition, bone mineral density, frailty score, balance ability, short physical performance battery, timed up-and-go test, activities of daily living). OSO patients will undergo a combined exercise intervention primarily based on resistance training in hospital and community settings for 12 months. Most older adults lack regular physical activity, leading to progressive muscle atrophy, impaired physical function, and substantially limited daily mobility. This initiates a vicious cycle wherein frailty, poor physical performance, sarcopenia, osteoporosis and adiposity reinforce each other, rendering structured exercise training extremely difficult for older adults. Unlike conventional combined training regimens that simply stack independent exercise modalities, this study implemented a hybrid multimodal exercise intervention. Hybrid multimodal exercise training (HMET) is a 12-month, supervised, progressive structured exercise intervention that systematically integrates resistance training, aerobic training, balance training, and flexibility training. It is designed to improve musculoskeletal strength, bone mineral density, body composition, and functional outcomes following enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) in patients with osteosarcopenic obesity (OSO). The four components are allocated within each training session according to a prespecified ratio, with periodic progression of training load to sustain adaptive responses.Characterized by low entry barriers, the intervention is easy for older adults to start, well-suited to daily life, and requires little specialized equipment. Patient functional status will be assessed using the Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illness and Loss of Weight Index (FRAIL), Tinetti Performance Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA), Timed Up and Go Test (TUG), Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), and Activities of Daily Living (ADL) scale. Body composition will be measured by multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis. Bone quality will be assessed by measuring vertebral HU values using energy CT, and bone mineral density T-scores of the lumbar spine and femoral neck will be analyzed by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA).
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Our study protocol has been registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR), a primary registry of the WHO International Clinical Trial Registry Platform (ICTRP). Registration website: https://www.chictr.org.cn/. Registration number: ChiCTR2600116975. The study protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP) are available on this website.

title: Therapeutic Potential of Plant-Derived Exosome-Like Nanovesicles in Musculoskeletal Disorders: Osteoporosis, Osteoarthritis, Bone Repair, and Skeletal Muscle Recovery.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders, including osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, impaired fracture healing, inflammatory bone loss, and sarcopenia, are major drivers of pain, frailty, falls, disability, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although current pharmacological interventions can inhibit bone resorption, relieve pain, or suppress inflammation, their clinical impact is often constrained by limited regenerative efficacy, suboptimal tissue targeting, long-term safety concerns, and insufficient capacity to address the multifactorial nature of chronic musculoskeletal disease. Plant-derived exosome-like nanovesicles (PELNVs), also referred to as plant-derived extracellular vesicles or exosome-like nanoparticles, have emerged as naturally organized lipid-bilayer nanoplatforms enriched in bioactive lipids, proteins, small RNAs, metabolites, and phytochemicals. These intrinsic features position PELNVs at the intersection of natural-product pharmacology, regenerative medicine, and nanoscale drug delivery. Accumulating evidence suggests that PELNVs derived from yam, ginseng, plum, Pueraria lobata, Morinda officinalis, Lycium barbarum, Drynaria roosii, watercress, grape skin, Chinese leek, and other edible or medicinal plants can modulate key processes involved in musculoskeletal homeostasis, including osteoblastogenesis, osteoclastogenesis, bone marrow mesenchymal stem-cell fate determination, chondrocyte senescence, mitochondrial quality control, inflammatory signaling, gut microbiota-derived metabolism, and skeletal muscle remodeling. In parallel, engineering approaches such as bone-targeting peptide conjugation, cartilage-binding peptide functionalization, chitosan-based shell assembly, hydrogel encapsulation, microneedle-assisted delivery, and localized depot systems are transforming PELNVs from crude vesicle preparations into programmable bio-organic therapeutic platforms. This review summarizes current evidence for the application of PELNVs in osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, bone and alveolar socket repair, inflammatory bone loss, muscle atrophy, sarcopenia, and exercise-related recovery, with particular emphasis on mechanistic insights, delivery strategies, translational challenges, and future standards for preclinical development. Oral bioavailability, causal cargo attribution, long-term safety, and manufacturing reproducibility remain unresolved.

title: Revisiting the Role of the Long Head of the Biceps in Shoulder Stability.
abstract: The long head of the biceps (LHB) tendon has traditionally been regarded as an expendable structure in shoulder surgery, often sacrificed without significant functional consequence. Histologic studies identify neural elements within the LHB and therefore provide biologic plausibility for afferent signaling; however, they do not establish an independent or clinically important contribution to proprioception. Cadaveric biomechanical studies demonstrate that applied LHB loading can resist humeral head translation, assist joint centering, and share load with capsulolabral structures under specific experimental conditions. Conversely, electromyographic and clinical studies show limited routine LHB recruitment during isolated shoulder motion and generally favorable outcomes after tenotomy or tenodesis. The evidence therefore supports a context-dependent model in which the LHB functions as a secondary stabilizer whose relevance varies with arm position, pathology, patient demands, and the integrity of surrounding structures. The LHB should be viewed as neither universally expendable nor universally essential, and surgical decisions should balance the dominant pain generator against the potential mechanical contribution of the tendon in the individual shoulder.

title: Sexual dimorphism in morphological predictors of upper- and lower-limb strength in adult rugby players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sex differences in athletic performance extend beyond body size, encompassing morphology-strength relationships.
AIM: To analyse sex-specific associations between body size and composition (body mass, fat-free mass [FFM], and thigh volume) and strength (hand grip strength and isokinetic knee extensor and flexor strength) in adult rugby players.
SUBJECTS AND METHODS: 84 players (42 males) were assessed. Body composition was measured by air-displacement plethysmography, and thigh volume was estimated anthropometrically. Strength was measured by grip (kg) and isokinetic knee torque at 60°·s-1.
RESULTS: Males were taller (178.3 cm), heavier (82.7 kg), and stronger (hand grip: 48.2 kg; knee extensors: 252 N·m). Females had a higher fat percentage (24.2% vs. 14.1%) and lower strength. FFM was the best predictor of peak torque in males (r ≈ 0.69 to 0.74); body mass correlated best (r ≈ 0.45 to 0.50) with peak torque in females. The hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio was, on average, 0.56 in both sexes.
CONCLUSION: Strength determinants differ by sex in rugby players. FFM is the primary predictor of strength in males, whereas body mass is more relevant in females. These findings support the development of sex-specific training methods to optimise performance and potentially reduce injury risk.

title: Combined Arthroscopic Hip Correction and Open Core Muscle Repair for Concomitant Femoroacetabular Impingement and Athletic Pubalgia: A Surgical Technique.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Concomitant femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) and core muscle injury (athletic pubalgia) represent an increasingly recognized source of persistent hip and groin pain in young athletes, with up to 94% of professional athletes with symptomatic FAI demonstrating signs of athletic pubalgia. Biomechanical alterations from FAI-particularly restricted hip internal rotation and compensatory pelvic mechanics-may predispose athletes to core muscle pathology. Isolated treatment yields suboptimal outcomes, with return-to-sport rates of 25% to 50% when only 1 pathology is addressed. We present the surgical technique for concurrent open core muscle repair and hip arthroscopy in a high-level athlete.
TECHNIQUE DESCRIPTION: The procedure is performed in 2 stages under a single anesthetic. Core muscle repair is performed first with the patient supine. A standard inguinal incision identifies external oblique fascial pathology. Full-thickness adductor longus tenotomy is performed at the pubic insertion. Ilioinguinal neurectomy is completed, followed by rectus muscle lateralization and reinforcement using interrupted permanent sutures to the pubic tubercle and iliopubic tract. After fascial closure, the patient is repositioned for hip arthroscopy, with standard anterolateral and mid-anterior portals, labral repair, femoroplasty for cam correction, and complete capsular closure.
RESULTS: Combined management of FAI and athletic pubalgia demonstrates superior outcomes compared with isolated treatment, with return-to-sport rates of 89% to 100% when both pathologies are addressed versus 25% to 50% for single-pathology treatment. All patient-reported outcome measures improve significantly after combined procedures. While treating FAI alone may successfully manage dual pathology in select patients, those with prominent core symptoms and imaging findings typically require formal core repair for optimal results.
CONCLUSION: In competitive athletes with persistent hip and groin pain, failure to recognize and address concomitant FAI and core muscle injury leads to incomplete symptom resolution and compromised performance. A biomechanical assessment revealing restricted hip internal rotation combined with core tenderness and pubic bone edema on magnetic resonance imaging should prompt evaluation for dual pathology. Combined surgical treatment under a single anesthetic represents a single-stage approach that optimizes outcomes and facilitates full return to competitive athletics in appropriately selected patients.

If the individual may be identifiable, the author(s) has included a statement of release or other written form of approval from the patient(s) with this submission for publication.

title: The Mechanical Regulatory Window of Cartilage Metabolism in Knee Osteoarthritis: From Mechanosensation to Parameter-Based Intervention Design.
abstract: Mechanical loading occupies a paradoxical position in osteoarthritis (OA): it contributes to cartilage degeneration, yet exercise is an established component of conservative OA care. This review advances the concept of a mechanical regulatory window of cartilage metabolism, a hypothesis-generating framework relating the magnitude, frequency, duration and mode of mechanical signals to chondrocyte metabolic responses. We synthesize evidence from the chondrocyte mechanosensory apparatus: ion channels and hemichannels, integrin-mediated adhesion, primary cilium-dependent signaling, and the pericellular matrix, to examine how their engagement under different loading conditions influences matrix homeostasis and catabolism. TRPV4 and PIEZO1/2 have context-dependent functions; inflammatory mediators can alter channel expression and amplify deformation-associated cellular injury. The window position may vary with disease state, inflammatory milieu, pericellular matrix properties and loading history. Tensile strain, construct compression, single-cell compression and substrate stiffness describe different physical inputs, and their numerical values cannot define a shared loading threshold. We identify three barriers to clinical translation: limited measurement of chondrocyte-level mechanical signals during treatment, incomplete mapping of mechanosensory signaling, and inconsistent parameter reporting across mechanical intervention studies. Addressing these gaps could support the rational design of mechanical interventions for OA. The proposed window remains to be validated against sustained cartilage and patient outcomes.

title: The Over-the-Top Technique Promotes Early Femoral Tendon-Soft Tissue Healing and Tibial Tendon-Bone Integration: An Experimental Study in Rabbits.
abstract: This study compared femoral graft healing and inflammatory responses following over-the-top (OTT) versus anatomical single-bundle (ASB) ACL reconstruction in 40 rabbits. Evaluations at 4, 8, and 12 weeks utilized histology, immunohistochemistry, ELISA, and biomechanical testing. Results showed OTT reconstruction, avoiding femoral tunnels, healed via tendon-soft tissue integration with dense fibrous connections by 4-8 weeks. Conversely, ASB healing occurred within tunnels, developing a classic four-layer enthesis by week 12. Type II collagen was significantly higher in OTT at week 4 but lower at week 8 (P<0.05). OTT grafts exhibited less edema and significantly lower synovial MMP-13 at week 4 (P<0.05). Biomechanically, OTT demonstrated superior maximum failure load at week 4 (65.5 N vs. 56.8 N, P=0.04), converging with ASB by week 12. Consequently, OTT reconstruction offers faster early integration, superior initial strength, and reduced early inflammation compared to the slower, classical enthesis pathway of ASB. These findings clarify OTT's distinct healing mechanism, supporting its clinical application for early rehabilitation, though clinical validation remains necessary.

title: Hydrogels as drug carriers for cartilage repair in osteoarthritis: Applications and challenges.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent chronic degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive cartilage degradation, subchondral bone remodelling, synovial inflammation, osteophyte formation, and loss of joint function, resulting in significant pain, disability, and socioeconomic burden worldwide. Despite advances in clinical management, current therapeutic strategies, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids, hyaluronic acid injections, and surgical interventions, primarily provide symptomatic relief and have limited ability to prevent disease progression or regenerate damaged cartilage. In recent years, hydrogel-based drug delivery systems have emerged as promising therapeutic platforms owing to their excellent biocompatibility, biodegradability, injectability, high water content, and structural similarity to the native extracellular matrix. These properties enable hydrogels to serve as effective carriers for a wide range of therapeutic agents, including anti-inflammatory drugs, growth factors, nucleic acids, nanoparticles, exosomes, and stem cells, while providing sustained and localized drug release within the osteoarthritic joint. This review comprehensively discusses the pathophysiology of OA and highlights the major molecular signaling pathways involved in disease progression, including NF-κB, MAPK, Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, TGF-β, and JAK/STAT pathways. Furthermore, recent advances in natural, synthetic, hybrid, and stimuli-responsive hydrogels are critically examined, with particular emphasis on their applications in cartilage repair and targeted drug delivery. Emerging approaches involving nanotechnology-enabled hydrogels, gene delivery systems, stem cell-loaded constructs, and immunomodulatory biomaterials are also evaluated for their therapeutic potential and translational prospects. This review provides an integrated and up-to-date perspective on hydrogel-based strategies for cartilage regeneration and disease modification, highlighting their potential as next-generation therapeutic platforms for the long-term management of osteoarthritis.

title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

title: Subject-Specific Cardiovascular Signatures Revealed by Arterial Pulse Signals in Patients with Heart Diseases-Part I: General Cases.
abstract: Background/Objectives: This study evaluates whether cardiovascular (CV) parameters derived from noninvasive arterial pulse signals can capture subject-specific physiological characteristics and longitudinal changes in patients with diverse heart diseases. Method: Arterial pulse signals at the radial artery (RA) and carotid artery (CA) of each patient were successfully recorded from all 18 patients using micro-fabricated tactile sensors. Signal quality was screened before analysis, and the accepted signals were analyzed using a single-degree-of-freedom time-frequency (SDOF-TF) framework. Key CV parameters, including time-based indices-heart rate (HR), heart rate variability (HRV), respiration rate (RR), and respiration modulation (RM), as well as harmonic amplitudes and normalized arterial pulse waveform (APW)-were extracted from measurements at rest and post-exercise across three rehabilitation visits in 18 patients with heterogeneous CV conditions. Longitudinal changes in CV parameters within subjects and variability between subjects were assessed. Results: Compared with a healthy reference, the patients exhibited heterogeneous CV profiles, with lower HRV in all patients except one with AF, who showed elevated HRV, and generally reduced post-exercise CV responses. Higher-order harmonic amplitudes were attenuated at the RA, while CA-derived APW measurements showed greater sensitivity to systolic upstroke slope. Marked inter-subject variability was evident in at-rest CV parameters and 5-min post-exercise responses. Longitudinal CV responses varied across rehabilitation visits, potentially reflecting multiple contributing factors. Conclusions: The 100% pulse acquisition rate supports the feasibility of the tactile sensor technology for pulse measurement, and the combined sensor technology and SDOF-TF framework enable quantitative characterization of shared and individualized CV patterns in cardiac patients and their post-exercise recovery, including time-based indices, harmonic signatures, site-specific differences, and interactions among CV parameters. These findings warrant further investigation in larger cohorts with appropriate physiological reference measurements.

title: The impact of mindfulness on sleep, cognitive function and athletic performance of young males migrating to the plateau.
abstract:
AIMS: To examine whether an 8-week mindfulness training program was associated with changes in sleep quality, cognitive function, and athletic performance in young men who migrated to high-altitude regions.
METHODS: Ninety-six young male migrants were randomly assigned to an 8-week mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) program (n = 48) or a no-intervention control group (n = 48). Sleep quality (PSQI), cognitive processing (P300 latency), and athletic performance (3000-m run time) were assessed before and after the intervention.
RESULTS: The mindfulness group was associated with greater improvements in sleep quality (PSQI median: 7.5 to 5 vs. 8 to 8.5, P < 0.001) and cognitive processing speed (P300 latency median: 387 ms to 357 ms vs. 376.5 ms to 374.5 ms, P = 0.01) compared with controls. Exploratory analyses suggested that P300 amplitude increased in parietal and occipital regions. No significant between-group difference was observed in 3000-m run completion time (P = 0.51) or grade improvement rates (25.0% vs. 29.17%, P = 0.65).
CONCLUSION: An 8-week mindfulness intervention was associated with improved sleep quality and cognitive processing speed, but no significant association was observed with athletic performance, in young male migrants to high-altitude regions. These preliminary findings suggest potential benefits of mindfulness as a non-pharmacological strategy for high-altitude health management, pending replication with active control conditions.

title: Changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health across training phases in elite Chinese artistic swimmers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Low energy availability (LEA) adversely affects athletes'physiological health, yet studies in elite synchronized swimmers across different pre-competition training phases are scarce. This study evaluated changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health in Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers before the National Games.
METHODS: Ten Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers sequentially completed a 1-week tapering phase (TP) and a 4-week intensified training phase (ITP). At the end of each phase, dietary intake (weighed food records), exercise energy expenditure (heart rate monitoring), energy availability (EA), resting metabolic rate (RMR), body composition, and blood biomarkers were measured. Within each training phase, athletes were classified into LEA and non-LEA groups according to their EA levels, and between-group differences were compared. In addition, overall changes between TP and ITP were analyzed in the full cohort of 10 athletes.
RESULTS: LEA prevalence was 40% during the TP and 60% during the ITP. In unadjusted analyzes, the LEA group showed significantly lower EI (p = 0.025), VO₂ (p = 0.022), mRMR (p = 0.023), RMR ratio (p = 0.006), and intakes of carbohydrate (p = 0.023), protein (p = 0.015), fat (p = 0.032), calcium (p = 0.038), and iron (p = 0.044) during the TP, with large effect-size estimates. As expected from the classification criteria, EA was significantly lower in the LEA group during both the TP (p = 0.001) and ITP (p = 0.005). During the ITP, fat (p = 0.027) and zinc intakes (p = 0.036) were significantly lower in the LEA group, whereas carbohydrate and protein intakes were lower but did not reach statistical significance. In the overall cohort, EEE (p < 0.001) and T4 (p = 0.010) increased from TP to ITP, whereas ferritin (p = 0.012) and calcium intake (p = 0.007) decreased, with large effect-size estimates.
CONCLUSION: During intensified training, EEE increased without a corresponding increase in EI, suggesting that dietary intake may not have adequately matched the increased training demands and may have increased susceptibility to LEA. LEA was associated with lower energy and macronutrient intakes, potential calcium and iron inadequacies, and phase-specific reductions in RMR-related measures. Phase-related biomarker changes could not be attributed specifically to LEA. Individualized and periodized nutritional monitoring and intervention are recommended to better align energy and nutrient intake with training demands and support athlete health and performance.

title: Dysphagia as the Initial Manifestation of Anti-HMGCR Antibody-Positive Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy Complicated by Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a rare autoimmune myopathy characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase levels. Although commonly associated with prior statin exposure, statin-naïve cases and atypical presentations are well described. Patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are also at increased risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), though data specific to IMNM remain limited.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 83-year-old man with brief, remote statin exposure presented with progressive proximal muscle weakness and a three-year history of oropharyngeal dysphagia preceding limb involvement. Laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated creatine kinase and transaminases. Anti-HMGCR antibodies were positive, and muscle biopsy confirmed necrotizing myopathy. During evaluation for occult malignancy, bilateral pulmonary emboli were incidentally identified. The patient required high-dose corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease. With aggressive immunosuppressive therapy and rehabilitation, he demonstrated substantial clinical recovery at 6 months.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights oropharyngeal dysphagia as an early and, for a prolonged period, isolated manifestation of anti-HMGCR antibody-positive IMNM; here, it preceded the onset of limb weakness by approximately 3 years. It underscores the importance of comprehensive diagnostic evaluation in patients with unexplained oropharyngeal dysfunction, in whom an inflammatory myopathy may otherwise be overlooked for years. Clinicians should maintain awareness of thrombotic risk in inflammatory myopathies, particularly during active disease. Early recognition and prompt immunosuppressive therapy remain critical to optimize outcomes and prevent irreversible muscle damage.

title: Vertical jump landing kinetics may be more sensitive to delayed-onset muscle soreness effects than forward and drop jumps.
abstract: Exercise-induced delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) may reduce joint range of motion and transiently impair muscle strength. However, DOMS-related symptoms do not consistently translate into measurable biomechanical changes in landing mechanics. Here we set out to determine whether exercise-induced DOMS alters landing kinetics in different landing tasks. Twenty-six physically active adults (15 women and 11 men) completed a squat protocol to induce lower extremity DOMS. Before and 48 h after the protocol, DOMS was assessed using a numerical pain rating scale, and the landing kinetics data were recorded during forward, vertical, and drop jumps. Joint stiffness and the joint contributions to the total support moment were determined and compared between baseline and DOMS conditions. DOMS significantly increased perceived muscle soreness and reduced vertical jump height by 16%. Joint stiffness did not differ between baseline and DOMS conditions for any landing task. Changes in total support moment (TSM) distribution were observed during vertical jump landings, with a reduced relative hip contribution at initial contact and an increased relative knee contribution at maximum knee flexion. No significant changes in TSM distribution were observed during forward or drop jump landings. These findings indicate that lower extremity DOMS may not necessarily alter overall landing stiffness but can modify inter-joint movement and torque strategies in vertical jump landing, highlighting the importance of evaluating movement mechanics alongside performance measures during recovery from strenuous exercise.

title: Genicular Artery Embolization for Knee Osteoarthritis: A Practical Guide and Future Directions on behalf of French Society of Rheumatology, Musculoskeletal Imaging Society, French Hip and Knee Society, French Society for Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, French Society of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine, and of French Society of Radiology.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To establish considerations for the indication and performance of genicular arteries embolization (GAE) for painful knee osteoarthritis on behalf of consortium of national societies.
METHODS: Based on literature review and clinical practice, a multidisciplinary group of 16 healthcare professionals including rheumatologists, interventional and MSK radiologists, physical and rehabilitation medicine physicians, knee orthopedic surgeons, and member of people living with OA association produced the considerations. Results : The group established 11 specific considerations. GAE is indicated for patients with painful knee osteoarthritis for whom no other cause of pain can be identified, and whose pain is refractory despite usual optimal medical treatment. A pre-therapeutic knee synovitis should be searched prior to GAE using a Doppler ultrasound or, even better, a contrast-enhanced MRI. Interventional radiologists should perform pre- and post-GAE consultations in collaboration with other musculoskeletal physician, in order to integrate GAE into the multimodal management strategy. Currently, there is no consensus on GAE techniques, and these should be individualized according to patient characteristics and interventional radiologist preferences. GAE may be repeated in selected cases. There are no contraindications to undergoing knee surgery after having GAE, but after a reasonable delay of three months. GAE may be considered in selected patients with persistent knee pain after knee replacement and after exclusion of other causes, including joint infection.
CONCLUSIONS: These considerations provide a structured guide for GAE in painful knee osteoarthritis. Several questions warrant further investigation through clinical or basic research.

title: Open Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis Debridement Augmented by Bioinductive Collagen Implant: Indications and Surgical Technique.
abstract: Lateral epicondylitis is a common cause of elbow pain that typically resolves with conservative management. For patients with persistent symptoms and failed nonoperative treatment, surgical intervention may be considered. We describe a surgical technique for open extensor carpi radialis brevis debridement with augmentation using a bovine-derived bioinductive collagen implant. The procedure involves direct visualization and excision of degenerative tendon, followed by extensor carpi radialis longus tendon repair using a suture anchor. A bioinductive patch is secured over the repair using absorbable staples and suture. This technique builds on principles established in rotator cuff repair, where bioinductive implants have shown increased tendon thickness, organized tissue regeneration, and reduced retear rates. Although no studies currently assess the efficacy of collagen augmentation in lateral epicondylitis, its hypothesized benefit lies in enhancing tendon healing and promoting growth of new tissue after debridement. Contraindications include active infection and allergy to implant materials. Postoperative rehabilitation includes early range of motion and gradual strengthening. This technique provides a reproducible approach to augment open extensor carpi radialis brevis debridement and warrants further studies to evaluate the effect of bioinductive patch augmentation and outcomes in patients with recalcitrant lateral epicondylitis.
